articles.title: I Broke My WSL, Nearly Lost 1.7 Million Files — A Digital Autopsy
articles.description:
TL;DR: Your drive is 100% full. You can't back up. You can't repair. You can only pray. And if you're lucky, the universe sends you an oracle card that says "Embracing Kindness" right when you're about to lose your mind. If you're unlucky, you meet a glass tube. Welcome to the read.
That morning, the sun was shining with a tone that seemed to say,
"Good morning, world. Everything is going to be fine."
I was sitting at my desk with a cup of coffee. Outside the window, leaves were swaying gently. Birds were chirping without sin. The universe seemed to have signed a peace treaty with me for that day.
I misread the contract. The contract was written in small print at the very bottom. The kind of contract you find in a predatory loan app with a 2%-per-day interest rate.
I — a developer who is also a carrot farmer — decided to install an AI agent that was trending. Because who needs a virtual machine when you can just run it directly in WSL?
"VMs are for paranoid people."
"WSL is for productive people."
"I'm a senior developer. I know what I'm doing."
"And if something breaks, I'll just restore from backup. Right?"
That last sentence would haunt me for the rest of my life.
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/.../install.sh
less install.sh
bash install.sh

The process ran. The terminal was colorful like a Christmas tree lit by someone who really, really loves colors. Downloading dependencies. Installing Node.js, Python, ripgrep, who knows what else. For a moment, I felt like I was watching a digital orchestra performing the symphony of human progress.
Then.
Hang.
Error.
Ctrl+C.
Dam*miT
Close terminal.
"Ah, just run it again, probably."
"Sometimes installs need a second try."
"Microsoft is weird sometimes, but they won't destroy my system."
"And if something breaks, I'll just restore from backup. Right?"
That sentence again. The same sentence. The sentence I said without knowing that the backup did not exist. Never existed. Will never exist. Because my drive was full, and I already knew that, but I chose not to think about it because thinking about it made me uncomfortable.
And there was one more thing I didn't think about. One thing that, if I had just thought about it for five seconds, might have prevented this entire disaster.
I didn't know where my VHDX was stored.
WSL never tells you. No installer asks. No notification pops up in the taskbar. The VHDX just... exists. Somewhere. Inside your computer. Maybe on drive C. Maybe on drive D. Maybe on drive E. I had moved mine two years ago, back when I thought drive C was too full. But I didn't remember where to. And after two years, I stopped asking.
"The VHDX is an abstraction."
"The VHDX is an implementation detail."
"The VHDX is not my problem. My problem is writing code."
And when that abstraction broke, I only then realized that the abstraction stood on top of a drive that was already full.
I opened WSL again.
And there, my life changed.
<3>WSL (124 - Relay) ERROR: CreateProcessParseCommon:996: getpwnam(jack) failed 5
<3>WSL (124 - Relay) ERROR: CreateProcessParseCommon:1005: getpwuid(1000) failed 5
<3>WSL (124 - Relay) ERROR: ConfigUpdateLanguage:2553: fopen(/etc/default/locale) failed 5
<3>WSL (124 - Relay) ERROR: operator():579: getpwuid(0) failed 5
wsl: Failed to start the systemd user session for 'root'. See journalctl for more details.
<3>WSL (124) ERROR: I/O error @util.cpp:1358 (UtilInitGroups)
<3>WSL (124 - Relay) ERROR: CreateProcessCommon:807: Create process failed

I read it. Once. Twice. Three times.
And the only thing that ran through my head was:
"I just destroyed five years of my life with one bash command, and there is no backup."
"I just committed digital suicide."
"Welcome to hell. Population: one."

The first reaction of every developer when facing a problem is to believe the problem is a lie. That maybe, if we close our eyes and open them again, reality will change. That Microsoft is just joking.
wsl --shutdown
wsl

The answer?
Catastrophic failure
Error code: Wsl/Service/E_UNEXPECTED

"Catastrophic failure."
Microsoft really chose the right words. Very poetic. Very dramatic. Very aligned with the state of my heart. The word "catastrophic" comes from the Greek katastrophē, meaning "an overturning" or "a destruction." In Ancient Rome, it meant "the end of a drama."
Which, in developer language, means:
"You just lost, bro. Enjoy the rest of your life."
"Catastrophic failure. Two words in English that I will remember until I die."
"If this were a movie, this scene would be scored with violins played by a child in the middle of a ruined city."
I checked the WSL version. 2.6.3.0. Oh, so we just upgraded to a version that... is a bit problematic. Great. Very great. Like buying a new car, and when you drive off the lot, the wheels are already off.
I tried wsl --update.
The older version of Windows Subsystem for Linux cannot be removed.
Update failed (exit code: 1603).

"The older version of Windows Subsystem for Linux cannot be removed."
Excuse me, Microsoft. I never asked you to remove the older version. I only asked you to update it. But it seems the universe has decided that today, I must learn the meaning of the word "helplessness."
"Maybe this is the universe's way of telling me it's time to switch to a MacBook."
"Or give up on technology and become a full-time carrot farmer."
"Carrots never say 'cannot be removed'."
"Carrots never say 'Catastrophic failure'."
"Carrots only say: water, soil, sunlight."
"And carrots never destroy my life because of a failed update."
I opened the log file Microsoft provided at C:\Users\...\AppData\Local\Temp\wsl-install-logs.txt.
It was 500 lines. I scrolled. I scrolled again. There were hundreds of lines like:
MSI (s) (18:98) [09:12:11:134]: Using cached product context: machine assigned for product: F993DD9E3A12E9747AFD6DFCB4A2BD3F

"F993DD9E3A12E9747AFD6DFCB4A2BD3F. What is this? The combination to a Swiss bank vault?"
"Or maybe it's my ex's phone number? Equally useless."
"Or is this a secret code to summon a demon? If so, I'm ready. I need help from dark forces."
But among the hundreds of lines, one caught my attention:
Property(S): OutOfDiskSpace = 0

Zero. Which means... no space issue.
Huh?
"OutOfDiskSpace = 0. So this isn't a space issue?"
"Microsoft, please don't lie to me at a time like this."
"I've suffered enough. Don't add lies to the pile."
"I've already lost five years of my life. Don't add illusions to it."
I closed the log. I sat in silence. Something was off. There was something Microsoft wasn't telling me. Something that even the MSI installer itself couldn't detect. Something hidden behind those hexadecimal numbers.
Then I remembered — I had never actually checked my drives.
And that was the moment I realized that this wasn't a disaster. This was a murder. And the perpetrator was me.
df -h — The Moment I Looked in the Mirror and Saw a Killer


I opened the old WSL terminal that somehow was still running as root, and typed a simple command:
df -h

And the output was one of the most shameful moments of my life as a developer.
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
C:\             101G   96G  5.0G  96% /mnt/c
D:\             137G  137G  1.5M 100% /mnt/d
E:\             112G  106G  5.6G  96% /mnt/e
/dev/sdd       1007G   83G  873G   9% /

I stared at the numbers. I re-read them. I hoped I had read them wrong.
D:\ — 137G used, 1.5 MB available, 100%.
1.5 MB.
Not 1.5 GB. Not 15 GB. 1.5 MB.
That's smaller than a low-res selfie. Smaller than a bad-bitrate MP3. Smaller than the log file I had just read. Smaller than the screenshot I had taken for remembrance. Smaller than an empty .txt file I had never written to.
And on that drive — a drive filled down to the last 1.5 MB — my VHDX was stored. The VHDX that held 1.7 million files. The VHDX that held five years of my life.
"Oh. Oh no."
"So it wasn't the install script that corrupted my filesystem."
"It wasn't Microsoft that destroyed my VHDX."
"It was me."
"I destroyed it."
"I am the murderer of my own data."
I closed my eyes. I closed my laptop. I looked at my carrot garden through the window.
Those carrots were growing peacefully. None of them were full. None of them had errors. None of them said Catastrophic failure. They only needed soil, water, and sunlight. And they always had room to grow.
I, on the other hand, was a developer who had let his D: drive fill to 100%. Down to 1.5 MB. And then I ran an installation script that needed to write hundreds of megabytes into a filesystem running on a drive that had no room left.
"That's like trying to pour water into a glass that's already full, then blaming the glass when the water spills."
"That's like pouring gasoline into a car with no tank, then blaming the engine when it won't start."
"That's like burying someone alive, then blaming the soil for being too dense."
"Enough. I understand now. I am the cause."
And this was the most painful moment. Because at that point, I also realized:
If my drive is full, I cannot make a backup.
To back up an 83 GB VHDX, I need 83 GB of free space. Drive D had 0 GB left. Drive C had 5 GB left. Drive E had 5.6 GB left.
So if I chose not to repair the VHDX, I would lose the data.
And if I chose to repair the VHDX, and something went wrong, I would lose the data.
I was trapped between two possible losses, and I couldn't avoid either one.
This was no longer a story about errors. This was a story about regret. A story about how we can become the executioner of our own lives without realizing it.
"If only I had deleted those pirated movies two weeks ago."
"If only I had moved those old downloads to an external drive."
"If only I had set aside 100 GB. Just 100 GB. For emergencies."
"If only I weren't lazy."
"If only I hadn't thought 'later'."
"If only, if only, if only."
Three of the most painful words in the human language.

If you use WSL and don't know where your VHDX is, this is the time to wake up. Most WSL users never know where their VHDX lives. The default:
C:\Users\<your-name>\AppData\Local\Packages\<Distro>\LocalState\ext4.vhdx

Example for Ubuntu from Microsoft Store:
C:\Users\lenovo\AppData\Local\Packages\CanonicalGroupLimited.Ubuntu_79rhkp1fndgsc\LocalState\ext4.vhdx

And for a manually imported distro (like mine):
D:\Kotonk\WSL\ext4.vhdx   (or wherever you put it)

Why this matters: If you don't know where your VHDX is, you won't know which drive to keep free. And if that drive fills up, you'll have the same nightmare as I did.
How to find your VHDX:
In PowerShell:
Get-ChildItem -Path "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Packages" -Filter "ext4.vhdx" -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object FullName, Length

Or search all drives:
Get-ChildItem -Path "C:\", "D:\", "E:\" -Filter "ext4.vhdx" -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object FullName, Length

Write it down. In a notebook. Screenshot it. Stick it on your wall. Because in a crisis, you'll forget.
Before I decided to repair the VHDX the right way, I scoured the internet searching for "WSL recovery tool" and "ext4 repair Windows" and various combinations of words that made Google start showing me ads for SSDs and cloud backups.
Every tool I found was a different story, and every story ended with the same line:
"Register to continue."
"Enter your license key."
"Upgrade to Pro."
"Payment required."
"Enter your credit card."
"We will send a verification email to your registered address."
"Please allow 3-5 business days for processing."
"For faster service, please consider our premium plan."

I made a mental list. But this time, I won't name them. Because I don't want to be sued. I'll only call them by what they deserve to be called: hope sellers.
The Reader That Only Reads
A tool that promised to let me browse my broken files — for free. And it delivered. I could see every file, every folder, every config. I could see five years of my life — displayed beautifully on the screen. Old photos. Old code. Old documents I wrote at 3 AM while crying.
But to copy anything? To write anything back? "Upgrade to Pro."
"So I can see all my files, but I can't take them."
"That's like watching your ex through a café window."
"Enjoying the suffering that the law allows."
"And I'm pretty sure if I click 'Upgrade', it will ask for my home address. And my mother's maiden name. And my blood type."
The Wizard With the Smiling Ads
A recovery tool whose YouTube ads are full of happy models. They smile. They seem to say: "If you use our product, your life will be as happy as ours." They don't know that I'm crying in front of my laptop.
I downloaded it. I installed it. The scan ran. Result? "42 files found!"
Oh. That was just the dummy files. To see the real files: pay. To save the recovery: pay. To close the app without feeling guilty: impossible, because it will show you a 30% discount popup that's only valid "today only."
"You know, I don't mind paying."
"But I want to know first if your tool can save my files."
"But you hide that behind a paywall."
"So we're both guessing. You're guessing I'll pay. I'm guessing your tool works."
"In this uncertainty, nobody wins. Except you, if I'm stupid."
The One That Needed a License
A tool that looked professional. Clean interface. Clear business model: you pay, we work. I downloaded. I installed. I opened. I selected the VHDX. And then:
"Recovery is only available in the Professional version. Please purchase a license."
I stared at the screen with a blank expression. I looked at my bank balance. I looked at my carrot garden outside. I looked at my neighbor watering his plants with calm.
"My neighbor is watering his plants."
"I'm watering my tears."
"And not a single one of them can be recovered from today."
The Forensic-Grade One
The kind of tool used by forensic labs and data recovery companies. The price for the Pro version? Hundreds of euros. For a carrot farmer who is also a developer, that's equivalent to several weeks of harvest.
I closed the tab. I wasn't angry. I understood. Every company has to eat. I have to eat too. I have bills too. I have carrots to sell at the market too.
But deep in my small heart, a voice whispered:
"If only you offered a 24-hour trial, I would be grateful for the rest of my life."
"But no. First, register your email."
"Verify. Enter your credit card."
"Consent to marketing emails from who knows how many companies."
"Provide your phone number."
"Provide your mother's maiden name."
"Provide your childhood home address."
"Provide your blood type."
"Provide three references from trustworthy friends."
"And after all that... 'Sorry, your VHDX file is not supported in the trial version.'"
"You know, I'm not asking for my files back for free."
"I'm only asking for a chance to try before I trust you with my money."
"But you treat me like a suspect who must show a credit card before being allowed into the interrogation room."
"Like I'm a thief trying to steal my own files."
The Free One From Ancient Times
It's free. Open source. Legendary. Everyone recommends it.
But... the documentation is an 800-page novel written by a man who really, really loves C. I read it. I tried to understand. I typed its name into the terminal.
And then I saw a white-text menu on a black screen that looked like it was from 1998.
"I'm not afraid of the command line."
"I'm just not sure that in the middle of my panic, I can navigate a menu that requires me to remember partition numbers."
"And if I press the wrong key, will I delete the partition that actually survived?"
"Will I change this story from 'I lost one file' to 'I lost everything'?"
"No. I don't want to take that risk."
"At least not before I write my will."
"And my will will say: 'To my wife, I leave my laptop. To my child, I leave my carrots. To Microsoft, I leave a curse.'"
I closed it. I took a deep breath. I returned to the terminal.
Decision: I would repair it myself. With my own hands. With knowledge that had long been buried in my head.
"Sometimes, the most ancient way is the most honest."
"And sometimes, the most ancient way is the only way left."
"Because all modern ways expect money I don't have."
"Or a sacrifice of data I don't want to give."
Every patient needs a hospital. And my VHDX — a file holding my entire digital life — was a dying patient.
I needed a "doctor." The doctor couldn't be Ubuntu (because Ubuntu was the broken one). So, I installed another distro: Debian.
Why Debian?
It's small (about 300 MB).
Stable as a rock.
Never dramatic.
Older than some of my colleagues.
And most importantly: it has no past with Microsoft Installer.




wsl --install -d Debian

Within a few minutes, my hospital was up. Complete with a new user, an easy-to-remember password, and a will of steel.
Now, I needed to bring the "patient" to this hospital.
wsl --shutdown
wsl --mount --vhd "D:\Kotonk\WSL\ext4.vhdx" --bare

Output: The operation completed successfully.
My first sigh of relief since that morning.

/dev/sdX Is a Myth


Here, I must admit. I made a big mistake by not thinking clearly.
I saw an online tutorial that said:
e2fsck -f -y /dev/sdX

And I — a senior developer who should have known better — ran that command as is.
e2fsck 1.47.2 (1-Jan-2025)
e2fsck: No such file or directory while trying to open /dev/sdX
Possibly non-existent device?

Of course there's nothing. /dev/sdX is a placeholder, not a device name. Using /dev/sdX is like looking for a file named filename.txt on a hard drive.
"If only the tutorials on the internet were a bit clearer, I wouldn't have spent the first ten minutes blaming Linux."
"But no. They write sdX assuming every reader already knows what it means."
"But every reader, especially one in a panic, won't know."
"And every second I spend guessing is a second bringing me closer to a heart attack."
Lesson one: Never trust a tutorial that uses sdX without explaining that you must replace it.
After I ran lsblk -f, it finally became clear:
NAME FSTYPE FSVER LABEL UUID                                 FSAVAIL FSUSE% MOUNTPOINTS
sda  ext4   1.0
sdb  ext4   1.0
sdc  swap   1           44ce0641-...
sdd  ext4   1.0         9f108056-7828-4919-8b8d-d5a755b8437c
sde  ext4   1.0         a048fd43-...                        955.3G     0% /mnt/wslg/distro

sdd. The device that's 1 TB, has type ext4, and no mountpoint.
That was it. My VHDX.
"sdd. Two letters and one number."
"That's what will determine whether I lose five years of my life or not."
"Sometimes I feel like life is unfair."
"Sometimes I feel like life is just a puzzle made by someone who really loves writing error messages."
"And sometimes I feel like I am a character in an unfunny joke, written by someone who doesn't like me."
e2fsck — The Moment I Prayed to God and the Linux Kernel Simultaneously


I took a breath. I placed my hands on the keyboard. I said words I hadn't said since my thesis defense:
"Lord, if my blessings are still in this file, please let them survive."
"If this is not the time for me to lose everything, please show me the way."
"If I still deserve to keep this data, please give me a second chance."
"I promise to back up. I promise to buy an external drive. I promise to delete those pirated movies."
And I pressed Enter.
wsl -d Debian -u root -- e2fsck -f -y /dev/sdd

The output flowed:
/dev/sdd: recovering journal
Pass 1: Checking inodes, blocks, and sizes
Pass 2: Checking directory structure
Pass 3: Checking directory connectivity
Pass 4: Checking reference counts
Pass 5: Checking group summary information
Free blocks count wrong (242242018, counted=242242017).
Fix? yes

Free inodes count wrong (65398741, counted=65398740).
Fix? yes

/dev/sdd: ***** FILE SYSTEM WAS MODIFIED *****
/dev/sdd: 1710124/67108864 files (0.2% non-contiguous), 26193439/268435456 blocks

1,710,124 files.
Not a hundred. Not a thousand. Not ten thousand.
One million, seven hundred ten thousand, one hundred twenty-four files.
And every one of them was still there.
I sat still. Didn't move. Didn't speak. I stared at the screen with the kind of gaze you might see in a father watching his child come home from war. The gaze of a man who just survived death. The gaze of a man who just realized that this world, though sometimes cruel, is also sometimes kind.
"They're still there. All of them are still there."
"Lord, I don't know what I did to deserve this, but thank you."
"I will never let my D: drive fill up again. I promise."
"I will delete those old files. I will move those pirated movies. I will buy an external drive."
"Even if I have to sell a few carrots at the market. By God, I will do it."
I picked up my coffee. Cold since two hours ago. I drank it. It was bitter. But for the first time that morning, I smiled.
When I tried to boot Ubuntu, the battle wasn't over.
wsl -d Ubuntu

wsl: Failed to start the systemd user session for 'jack'. See journalctl for more details.
<3>WSL (207 - Relay) ERROR: CreateProcessCommon:818: execvpe(/bin/bash) failed: I/O error

"Failed to start the systemd user session for 'jack'."
This is a known bug in WSL 2.6.x and 2.7.x. The systemd user session fails to start, so WSL can't execute /bin/bash as a regular user.
It's like having a car whose engine is healthy but whose ignition key is broken. You can see the car. You can touch it. You can cry next to it. But you can't start it.
"Of course. Of course there's another problem."
"If life were easy, maybe I'd be someone else."
"If life were easy, maybe I wouldn't have to write this article on dev.to."
"If life were easy, maybe I'd be a full-time carrot farmer, and I'd never know what 'Catastrophic failure' means."
The solution was simple but required courage: disable systemd temporarily.
I mounted the VHDX again, this time with auto-mount:
wsl --mount --vhd "D:\Kotonk\WSL\ext4.vhdx"

And then... something funny happened.
The disk was successfully mounted as '/mnt/wsl/DKotonkWSLext4vhdx'.

Notice the path: /mnt/wsl/DKotonkWSLext4vhdx.
Microsoft concatenated the entire path D:\Kotonk\WSL\ext4.vhdx into a single folder name without separators.
"Microsoft. You are geniuses in many ways."
"But there are some things that make me sure you made this decision on a Friday afternoon, five minutes before going home."
"Or maybe you did it on purpose. To test the patience of humanity."
"If so, you succeeded. Congratulations. I surrender. I will become a full-time carrot farmer."
I verified /bin/bash:
ls -la /mnt/wsl/DKotonkWSLext4vhdx/bin/bash
-rwxr-xr-x 1 root root 1446024 Mar 31  2024 /mnt/wsl/DKotonkWSLext4vhdx/bin/bash

There. Healthy. 1.4 MB.
I disabled systemd:
bash -c "echo '[boot]' > /mnt/wsl/DKotonkWSLext4vhdx/etc/wsl.conf && \
         echo 'systemd=false' >> /mnt/wsl/DKotonkWSLext4vhdx/etc/wsl.conf"

Unmount. Boot Ubuntu.
And...
Welcome to Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS.
Ubuntu booted. But I logged in as root, not jack. And the old error about /etc/default/locale still haunted me.
From inside the root shell, I ran cleanup operations:
grep jack /etc/passwd
# jack:x:1000:1000:,,,:/home/jack:/bin/bash   <- user still exists!

ls -la /home/ | grep jack
# drwxr-x--- 79 jack jack 4096 Sep 29 05:14 jack   <- ownership correct!

echo 'LANG=en_US.UTF-8' > /etc/default/locale
cat /etc/default/locale
# LANG=en_US.UTF-8

All green. User jack exists. Home has 79 folders. Permissions correct.
"79 folders. How many years of work do these 79 folders represent?"
"I don't know. I don't want to count. I'll get sad again."
"And I've been sad enough for today. Enough for this week. Enough for this month."
Exit the root shell. In PowerShell:
wsl --shutdown
wsl --manage Ubuntu --set-default-user jack
# The operation completed successfully.
wsl

And...
╭─jack@Jack 🕒 Tue Sep 29 12:08:26 📁 /mnt/c/Users/lenovo ✅

Jack. Not root. All files intact. All normal.
And I, for the first time that morning, genuinely smiled. Not a bitter smile. Not a cynical smile. A sincere smile.
"We won."
"Not a big victory. Not a victory that will be remembered in history."
"But a victory that is enough."
"And sometimes, a victory that is enough is the best victory we can hope for."
df -h — When the Universe Slapped Me for the Second Time


I ran a few simple commands to make sure everything was fine:
cd ~
pwd
# /home/jack

uname -a
# Linux Jack 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2

whoami
# jack

df -h

And there, I saw again something that made me sigh deeply:
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
C:\             101G   96G  5.0G  96% /mnt/c
D:\             137G  137G  1.5M 100% /mnt/d
E:\             112G  106G  5.6G  96% /mnt/e
/dev/sdd       1007G   83G  873G   9% /

D:\ is still 100% full. C:\ is still 96%. E:\ is still 96%.
That day, I had repaired my WSL. But the root cause is still there.
"This disaster isn't really over."
"This disaster is just waiting for its next chance to happen again."
"If I don't clean my drives, this will happen again."
"Maybe not this week. Maybe not this month."
"But it will happen again."
"And I have to decide: will I let my drives fill until they die, or will I do something about it?"
I closed my laptop. I went outside. I walked to the back garden. The evening breeze blew gently. The sun was starting to set. And for some reason, in the middle of that silence, I remembered someone who had drawn a card for me that day.
I'm not a superstitious person. I'm a developer. I believe in logic, in e2fsck, in lines of code that run as instructed. I believe problems have solutions, and solutions have documentation. I believe the universe consists of atoms and energy, not of signs and omens.
But that day, the universe seemed to be speaking through an unusual channel.
Someone I know — someone I respect — drew a card for me that day. And the card said:
"Embracing Kindness."
An angel with layered wings of purple, pink, and blue. Sitting in lotus position on a crescent moon. Around it, stars and cosmic nebulae. Below it, a white ribbon with the words: "Embracing Kindness."
The person who drew the card said:
"We are connected across space and time."
And for a moment, I was silent.
Because those words felt strange, but also very real. In the middle of all the 1603 errors, Catastrophic failure, and the dying VHDX, there was one simple message: Be kind to yourself.
"Space and time."
"Maybe it doesn't mean space and time literally."
"Maybe it means: in the middle of all this chaos, you still have time to forgive yourself."
"You still have time to stop blaming yourself for not backing up."
"You still have time to stop feeling stupid for letting your D: drive fill up."
"You still have time to stop feeling like a failure because of one bash install.sh command."
I looked at my carrots. They never blamed themselves when the soil was dry. They just grew. They just survived. They just waited for the next rain. They never said "Catastrophic failure." They never said "Contact your technical support group." They just grew, in silence, in a silence that never judged.
And I — a developer who is also a carrot farmer — realized something I might have known all along but always forgot.
We are all angels learning to embrace kindness. Even when we have just destroyed our own VHDX.
We are all angels sitting on a crescent moon, in the middle of cosmic chaos, trying to stay calm.
We are all angels whose wings are layered in color, even if sometimes we forget we have wings.
I smiled. I took a deep breath. I returned to my laptop.
And I wrote a note to myself in my notebook:
"Today, I almost lost 1.7 million files. But I didn't lose them. And today, I learned to forgive myself. Thank you, 'Embracing Kindness' card. Thank you, universe, for reminding me that in the middle of all this chaos, there is still room for kindness."
The next day, I opened WSL again. With a calm feeling. With a feeling that the storm had passed. With a feeling that I had paid a heavy price for a valuable lesson.
I opened my project. I ran sudo nano /etc/wsl.conf to fix some configuration. I ran ps -aux to see running processes. Everything was normal. Everything was calm.
Then I tried to run MySQL.
sudo service mysql start

mysql: unrecognized service

Oh. MySQL wasn't installed. Of course. Because my VHDX had just recovered. I had to reinstall some packages. I ran:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install mysql-server -y

The process ran. Downloading packages. Downloading indexes. Downloading metadata.
And then.
E: Failed to fetch http://security.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/... Could not create temporary file for /var/lib/apt/lists/partial/... - mkstemp (30: Read-only file system)

W: Problem unlinking the file /var/lib/apt/lists/... - TransactionAbort (30: Read-only file system)

E: Unable to mkstemp /tmp/clearsigned.message.Y4tvZn - GetTempFile (30: Read-only file system)

E: The package lists or status file could not be parsed or opened.

Read-only file system.
Three words that made my blood stop flowing.
I tried sudo systemctl start mysql:
sudo: systemctl: command not found

Of course. Because systemd was disabled. Because I disabled it yesterday.
Then I tried a simple command:
php -l scripts/migrate-all.php

-bash: /usr/bin/php: Input/output error
-bash: /usr/bin/direnv: Input/output error
-bash: /usr/bin/date: Input/output error
-bash: /usr/bin/sed: Input/output error

Input/output error. Input/output error. Input/output error.
I stared at the screen. I stared at those words. I stared at /usr/bin/date that couldn't be run. /usr/bin/sed that couldn't be run. Even date — the simplest command in the Linux world, a command that just shows the date and time — couldn't be run.
"No."
"No. No. No. No."
"I just fixed it yesterday. I just saved 1.7 million files. I just prayed to God and the Linux kernel. I just saw a tiny angel on a crescent moon. And now... now what is this?"
I tried pressing Ctrl+C. Couldn't. I tried closing the terminal. It kept appearing.
-bash: /usr/bin/direnv: Input/output error
-bash: /usr/bin/date: Input/output error
-bash: /usr/bin/sed: Input/output error

I tried again. Ctrl+C.
-bash: /usr/bin/direnv: Input/output error
-bash: /usr/bin/date: Input/output error
-bash: /usr/bin/sed: Input/output error

MY FILESYSTEM WAS READ-ONLY.
I sat in my chair. I stared at my screen. I stared at the ceiling. I stared at my carrot garden through the window. And I felt like I was watching a replay of everything I had been through yesterday, but this time with a crueler twist.
Yesterday, my filesystem was corrupt. I repaired it.
Today, my filesystem was locked. And I didn't know why.
I sat there for several minutes. Reflecting. Thinking. Trying to understand.
And then, I realized. I realized what was happening.
Drive D: was still full. 99%. 1.9 GB left. That wasn't enough.
Yesterday, I repaired the filesystem with e2fsck. But I didn't fix the root cause: drive D: was still too full to hold filesystem operations.
Every time I wrote to WSL — installing packages, editing files, running apt update — the filesystem tried to write to the VHDX. The VHDX tried to write to drive D:. Drive D: had no room. The Linux kernel, as a last-ditch defense mechanism, locked the filesystem into read-only. Not because the filesystem was corrupted. But because the host disk was full.
It's like a doctor saying: "I've healed your wound. But you're still in a room with no oxygen. So your wound will reopen."
Or more precisely:
My filesystem wasn't a broken glass tube. My filesystem was a glass tube locked tight from the outside, because drive D: was so full that no key could turn.
I saw the metaphor clearly. A beautiful glass tube, holding my entire digital life — files, photos, code, memories. But the lid was locked. Not because the tube was broken. Not because its contents were broken. But because there was no room to turn the key.
"Yesterday, I lost access to the tube because its contents were broken."
"Today, I lost access to the tube because the tube was locked tight."
"And the lock couldn't be turned because drive D: was full."
"I wasn't just the murderer of my own data."
"I was also the jailer of my own data."
"I locked that tube from the outside, and now I can't open it."
I laughed. A small laugh. A bitter laugh. The laugh of someone who no longer has tears left to cry.
"This is funny."
"This is really funny."
"The universe sent me a tiny angel on a crescent moon yesterday."
"And today, the universe sent me a glass tube locked tight."
"Maybe this is the universe saying: 'You haven't finished learning yet, kid.'"
"Maybe this is the universe saying: 'You've learned to forgive yourself. Now, learn to clean your room.'"
I closed my laptop. I stood up. I walked to drive D: in File Explorer. I saw the number I had seen many times before: 99% full. 1.9 GB free.
I stared at that number. I stared at it like an old enemy. An enemy I had defeated yesterday, but who returned today with the same face.
"Alright, D:."
"You won yesterday. You won today."
"But tomorrow, I will delete those files. I will move those movies. I will empty you down to 50%."
"And you will never be able to lock my glass tube again."

If you ever see an error like this:
-bash: /usr/bin/date: Input/output error
Could not create temporary file ... Read-only file system

This does NOT mean your filesystem is corrupt. It means the Linux kernel has locked your filesystem into read-only for one of two reasons:
The host disk is full — the drive where your VHDX is stored (e.g., drive D:) has no room to write. This is what happened to me.
The internal filesystem is corrupt — the ext4 filesystem inside the VHDX found an inconsistency it couldn't automatically repair, so the kernel decided to lock it to prevent further damage.
How to check for the first one:
In PowerShell (Windows):
# Check D: drive space
Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem | Select-Object Name, @{N='Used(GB)';E={[math]::Round($_.Used/1GB,2)}}, @{N='Free(GB)';E={[math]::Round($_.Free/1GB,2)}}

In WSL:
df -h /mnt/d

How to fix the first one: Free up space on drive D:. That's it. Once there's room, the filesystem can be remounted as read-write:
sudo mount -o remount,rw /

How to fix the second one: Run e2fsck from a rescue distro (as I did yesterday).
How to prevent both: Never let the drive hosting your VHDX fill above 90%. Leave at least 20-30 GB of breathing room. Because the Linux kernel doesn't politely tell you. It just locks your filesystem and says: "Read-only file system."
Now, my WSL runs fine. All files are there. My shell is beautiful with powerline icons. My coffee has been replaced with a new one — warm, though no longer the first cup. My D: drive is still 99% full, but I've promised myself I'll clean it. Tomorrow. Or the day after. Or next week. But I will do it.
And here, I want to close this story with something honest.
Throughout my life as a developer, I've experienced many things. Bugs that couldn't be reproduced. Clients asking for revisions at 11 PM. Deadlines that seemed to be made by the devil himself. I once stayed up 48 hours to fix a problem whose solution turned out to be a single character.
But these past two days — two days full of 1603 errors, Catastrophic failure, e2fsck, systemd, read-only filesystem, and a tiny angel on a crescent moon — these two days taught me something no book or tutorial ever could.
They taught me the meaning of vulnerability.
That everything we build — projects, careers, data, memories — can collapse in a single bash command. That a full drive can destroy five years of our life. That 1.5 MB can be the distance between safe and gone. That the universe isn't always fair. That technology, however advanced, still stands on fragile foundations: disk space, electricity, and luck.
And they also taught me the meaning of kindness.
That in the middle of all that chaos, there was an oracle card that said "Embracing Kindness." That there was a tiny angel sitting on a crescent moon, reminding me to forgive myself. That there were carrots in the back garden growing peacefully, not caring whether my WSL was broken.
That evening, I sat on the back porch, staring at my carrot garden. My neighbor passed by the front of the house, carrying a hoe. He saw me, and smiled.
"What's up with you?" he asked. "You look like you just came back from a war."
I smiled. I looked at my carrots. I looked at my closed laptop on my lap. I looked at the sky beginning to darken.
"My WSL broke," I answered casually. "But it's fixed now."
My neighbor didn't understand what WSL was. He didn't know what Linux, ext4, or VHDX meant. He was just a carrot farmer, like me — except he didn't write code. He nodded slowly, looked at my carrots, and said:
"Good. Your carrots look healthy."
And he continued on his way.
I stared at those carrots for a long time. Their green leaves swayed gently in the evening wind. The soil around them was dark and damp. Their roots, invisible, worked in silence to grow downward, piercing the earth, seeking water and nutrients.
"Yes."
"My carrots are healthy. My WSL is healthy. I am healthy."
"Maybe this is what peace feels like."
I close this story with something I will probably repeat to myself for the rest of my life:
We are all glass tubes. Our contents are fragile. Our lids can lock at any moment. And sometimes, we forget to keep space around us so that the key can turn.
We are all carrots. We grow in silence. We don't care whether the digital world above us is in chaos. We only need soil, water, and sunlight.
We are all tiny angels on a crescent moon. We have layered, colorful wings. We just often forget that we have wings.
And sometimes, the only thing we can do is forgive ourselves. And water the carrots.
To every developer who has ever lost data:
You are not alone. We have all been there. We have all sat in this chair, staring at a blank screen, feeling like the world is laughing at us.
But you will recover. Your files will recover. And one day, you will tell this story, and someone else will learn from your experience.
That's why we write. That's why we share. That's why we keep moving forward.
Stay sane. Stay backed up. And don't forget to water your carrots.
— jack, developer, carrot farmer, and tiny angel on a crescent moon learning to embrace kindness (and to keep the glass tube unlockable) 🖤🥕🌙
P.S.: If anyone knows why Microsoft doesn't provide wsl --repair-filesystem in 2026, please let me know. I'm collecting signatures for a petition. And maybe I'm also considering sending a letter to Satya Nadella. With attached photos of my carrot garden. And a photo of a glass tube locked shut. And a photo of a tiny angel on a crescent moon.
P.P.S.: If you have an idle external drive and want to donate it for my WSL backup, I will be grateful for the rest of my life. In return, I will send you a sack of carrots every harvest. Seriously. I'm not joking. This is not a dark joke. This is a real offer from a developer who just survived digital death twice in two days.
Disk Space Is the Foundation of Everything


This is the most painful lesson of all. If your drive is 96-100% full, you cannot:
Backup your VHDX (needs free space).
Update WSL (MSI needs room to extract).
Repair the filesystem (ext4 needs room for the journal).
Install new packages (which triggers corruption).
Run simple commands like date (because the filesystem becomes read-only).
Disk space is the foundation of all your operations. Nothing else matters more to preserve. Not CPU, not RAM, not GPU. Everything collapses when disk space runs out.
I learned this with the price of 5 years of data. Don't let yourself pay more than I did.
BACKUP. YOUR. VHDX.


This is not advice. This is a sacred command. ext4.vhdx is the only container of all your Linux data. If that file disappears, everything disappears. No "restore from git." No "just pull again." Gone. Permanently.
Minimum backup:
Zip /home/<user> to a .tar.gz archive periodically.
Push repos to GitHub every day.
Copy the VHDX to cloud storage even if it's slow.
Better backup:
Buy an external drive. A 1 TB external drive costs less than a few weeks of carrot harvest.
Copy the VHDX weekly.
Best backup:
Snapshot the VHDX before big experiments.
Automate daily backups via script.
Know Where Your VHDX Lives


Most WSL users don't know. The default is:
C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Packages\<distro>\LocalState\ext4.vhdx

Or, if you've moved it:
D:\<your-chosen-location>\ext4.vhdx

Write it down. In a notebook. Screenshot it. Print it. Stick it on the wall. Because in a crisis, you'll forget.
Know How to Rescue Your VHDX


Write this down in your notebook:
# 1. Mount the VHDX in a rescue distro
wsl --mount --vhd "D:\Kotonk\WSL\ext4.vhdx" --bare

# 2. Find the device (usually sdd, but DON'T ASSUME!)
wsl -d Debian -u root -- lsblk -f

# 3. Repair the filesystem (REPLACE /dev/sdd with the correct device!)
wsl -d Debian -u root -- e2fsck -f -y /dev/sdd

# 4. Unmount
wsl --unmount "D:\Kotonk\WSL\ext4.vhdx"

# 5. Boot again
wsl -d Ubuntu

# 6. If the filesystem is read-only:
wsl -d Ubuntu
sudo mount -o remount,rw /

Prepare a Rescue Distro Before the Crisis


I will never again be without Debian as my "hospital." It's only 300 MB. It functions like insurance.
wsl --install -d Debian

Do it now, not during the crisis.
Don't Install Random Scripts in Your Main WSL


Installation scripts from any project — however popular — can leave the filesystem in an inconsistent state mid-way. WSL is a production environment for many of us. Treat it like production:
Test in a VM first (VirtualBox, Hyper-V, Multipass).
Or in a container (Docker/Podman).
Or in a VHDX snapshot that can be rolled back.
Don't Trust Tutorials That Use /dev/sdX


I'll repeat: /dev/sdX is a placeholder, not a valid device name. Every time you see it in a tutorial, replace it with the device name that appears in your lsblk.
Read-Only Filesystem Doesn't Mean Corrupt


If you see a Read-only file system error, that's NOT the end of the world. It's a Linux kernel defense mechanism. First check if the host drive is full. If yes, free up space, then run sudo mount -o remount,rw /. If it's still read-only, then run e2fsck from a rescue distro.
Fin.

articles.title: Bridging Clinical Logic and LLMs: Engineering Safety into Dry Needling Workflows
articles.description:
When we talk about AI agents interacting with the physical world—even indirectly through clinical guidance—we move quickly from 'interesting chatbot' to 'high-stakes liability.' In medical domains, a hallucination isn't just a wrong fact; it is a potentially dangerous instruction.
I recently looked closely at how we handle specialized domain logic within the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem. Specifically, I wanted to examine the implementation of the Dry Needling Depth Calculator, a connector designed for practitioners managing myofascial trigger points. This isn't just another utility tool; it represents a specific challenge in prompt engineering and tool selection: How do you ensure an LLM respects physiological boundaries when calculating needle parameters?
Dry needling requires exactness. Practitioners must account for muscle thickness, target depths, and entry angles while strictly avoiding neurovascular structures. If an agent suggests a 30mm insertion for a tissue layer that is only 25mm thick, or fails to respect the proximity of a major nerve, the outcome is catastrophic.
A standard LLM might estimate these values reasonably well via probabilistic reasoning, but it lacks the deterministic guardrails required for clinical safety. To solve this, the connector shifts the heavy lifting from the LLM's latent space to dedicated, verifiable functions:
  get_insertion_parameters: Calculates depth, length, and angle based on input metrics.
  validate_safety_boundaries: Acts as the primary gatekeeper against neurovascular risks.
  calculate_needle_selection: Maps mathematical needs to physical hardware (needle sizes).
  get_anatomical_constraints: Adjusts calculations based on local anatomy like bone proximity.
The goal here is clear: use the LLM for intent recognition and conversational interface, but delegate all safety-critical math to defined tools.
Most developers starting with MCP build everything locally. They run a server on localhost, configure their client, and call it a day. That works for personal productivity hacks or playing with RAG pipelines. It falls apart when you want to deploy an agentic workflow that is reliable, secure, and accessible across different environments (like moving from Cursor to Claude Desktop or a custom enterprise orchestration engine).
This brings me back to why I built Vinkius. During my work developing MCPFusion—the TypeScript framework used to power this very connector—I realized that most people spend more time fighting OAuth callbacks and environment variables than they do refining their tool logic.
In a production context, having an agent interact with sensitive health data or provide critical instructions demands three things that standard community MCP servers often lack:
Single Gateway Access: Instead of configuring individual credentials for every single niche service, Vinkius allows you to use one connection token. This eliminates credential sprawl across multiple IDEs and clients.
Isolated Execution: When an agent calls validate_safety_boundaries, that computation doesn't happen in an unmanaged shell. On Vinkius, every connector runs in an isolated V8 sandbox. We implement eight distinct governance policies—including SSRF prevention and HMAC audit chains—to ensure that even if an agent attempts to exploit a tool call, the blast radius is contained.
essential for preventing unauthorized lateral movement within your infrastructure.
Consistent Tool Behavior: By using MCPFusion under the hood, we ensure that headers, error responses, and schema definitions remain consistent regardless of whether you are querying biological constraints or inventory management APIs.
The technical performance of such a specialized tool tells its own story. Looking at recent telemetry for this calculator, we see an average latency of roughly 940ms. While not instantaneous, this reflects the overhead of running validated computations within our sandboxed environment—a tradeoff I consider necessary for stability.
The debugger score sits at 100 (Grade A+), which indicates strict adherence to schema validation. For engineers building agents around this tool, this means you won't hit those frustrating runtime errors where the LLM sends a string instead of a float for muscle thickness; the underlying framework catches these discrepancies before they propagate through your application logic.
An example of how this looks in practice during an inference loop:
"Input: Calculate needle parameters for a muscle that is 30mm thick with a trigger point at 15mm depth."
The real test occurs when constraints conflict:
validate_safety_boundaries overrides any optimistic estimation provided by the LLM.', inspection reveals that correctly implemented tools act less like 'knowledge bases' and more like 'physics engines' for reality.\
AI agents only matter when they reach real systems. We built the connector catalog. Discover Vinkius.

articles.title: A hidden folder never reached our artifact and our app links opened in the browser
articles.description:
In May our mobile team asked why links in our emails had started opening the website instead of the app. It had been going on for eleven days.
Our website is a static build. One job builds it and uploads the output folder with actions/upload-artifact, and a deploy job downloads that artifact and runs aws s3 sync with the delete option into the bucket behind our CDN. Two of the files in that folder matter only to phones: .well-known/apple-app-site-association and .well-known/assetlinks.json. iOS and Android read them to decide that a link to our domain may open our app.
Our workflows referred to the upload action as v4, a tag that moves. A minor release of that action, 4.4.0, changed its default so that hidden files and directories, anything whose name starts with a dot, are left out of the artifact unless include-hidden-files is set. It was a sensible security change, made after researchers found artifacts carrying .git folders with credentials in them. Our next build produced an artifact without .well-known, and the upload step said nothing worth reading. Then the sync did exactly what the delete option is for. It removed from the bucket every file the source no longer had, including the two that had sat there for four years.
Every page still returned 200, and every test we had passed. Phones do not fetch those files on each tap. Apple serves them from its own CDN and refreshes its copy now and then, and Android checks them when an app is installed or updated. So the breakage spread phone by phone, and the first reports, from some users, were put down to settings on their phones.
include-hidden-files is now set explicitly. Every third party action is pinned to a full commit SHA, and the update bot opens a pull request with the release notes, so a default changes when somebody has read about it. The build writes a manifest of every file with its hash, and the deploy refuses an artifact that does not match it. Deletions are listed before the sync and capped at twenty files without a label. And after each deploy a check fetches both files from the public domain and fails unless they return JSON that names our app.
By convention a dot hides a file from people. Ours were the only two files on the site that no person ever reads.
– Sergey Shinder

articles.title: RepoDNA v1.3.2: A Dedicated Documentation Website and Reliability Improvements
articles.description:
Tags: opensource, rust, devtools, webdev
RepoDNA v1.3.2 is now available!
This release introduces a dedicated documentation website and improves several parts of the project's error handling, GitHub Actions downloads, and documentation workflow.
RepoDNA is an open-source, local-first repository intelligence and code archaeology tool. It helps developers explore code structure, architecture, dependencies, Git history, quality signals, and project evolution.
The goal is to make a repository easier to understand—not just easier to browse.
The documentation now has a dedicated home:
https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/docs/
The site brings together the project's guides, changelog, roadmap, policies, examples, benchmarks, and fixtures.
It includes:
Search across documentation sections.
A sidebar that follows the documentation index.
Previous and next page navigation.
Copy buttons for code examples.
Light and dark themes.
Responsive layouts for phones.
Print-friendly pages.
Links between related guides and repository files.
The documentation is published alongside the web version, making the guides easier to discover and navigate.
The repodna-wasm component now reports missing files and folders more clearly.
Previously, some invalid inputs could surface low-level Node.js errors or be treated as the wrong kind of input. The improved behavior explains what is missing and clarifies when commands such as report or card require an analysis file.
Temporary failures from GitHub's servers could cause downloads to fail after only a short period.
The GitHub Action now retries download attempts for up to two minutes and provides a more accurate error when a download actually fails.
The guide for the action has also been updated to include the security-only profile in its supported profile options.
The development and documentation workflows now check for broken links and anchors. This helps catch navigation problems before changes are released.
The project also updates documentation destinations and support links across the relevant application and repository pages.
Documentation is part of the developer experience. It should be easy to search, navigate, read on a small screen, and use while working through real development problems.
Likewise, errors should explain what went wrong, and automation should distinguish temporary infrastructure failures from genuinely missing files.
Those improvements make the project easier to explore and maintain.
Release notes:

https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA/releases/tag/v1.3.2
Documentation:

https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/docs/
Web version:

https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/
Source code:

https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA
RepoDNA remains focused on local-first analysis and evidence-backed findings, with optional AI explanations rather than AI as a requirement.
Feedback, testing, contributions, and ideas for future releases are welcome.


  
  
  RepoDNA #OpenSource #Rust #DeveloperTools

articles.title: How JWTs Work, and Why Decoding Is Not Verification
articles.description:
JSON Web Tokens are everywhere: authentication, single sign-on, API authorization. They are also one of the most misunderstood pieces of the modern web — mostly because people confuse decoding a token with verifying it.
Here is what is actually inside a JWT, and the one mistake that quietly turns a "secure" auth system into an open door.
A JWT is just a string with three dot-separated segments:
header.payload.signature

Header — the token type and the signing algorithm (e.g. HS256, RS256).
Payload — the claims: user ID, roles, expiry (exp), issuer (iss), audience (aud).
Signature — what lets a trusted party confirm the token was not tampered with.
The first two segments are Base64URL-encoded JSON. That is all. They are not encrypted, and anyone holding the token can read them.
This is the part that bites people.
Decoding a JWT reveals its contents — nothing more. It does not prove the token was issued by your server, or that it has not been modified.
To actually trust a token you must:
Verify the signature with the correct key or secret.
Check exp — the token has not expired.
Check iss and aud match what you expect.
Skip any of those and you have effectively built an API where anyone can mint themselves an admin token.
Sometimes you just want to see what is inside. The payload is Base64URL, so:
JavaScript
const [, payload] = token.split('.')
const json = JSON.parse(atob(payload.replace(/-/g, '+').replace(/_/g, '/')))
console.log(json)

Python
import base64, json

payload = token.split('.')[1]
padding = '=' * (-len(payload) % 4)
print(json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(payload + padding)))

PHP
[$header, $payload, $sig] = explode('.', $token);
echo base64_decode(strtr($payload, '-_', '+/'));

Note that none of these snippets verify anything — they only decode.
Putting secrets in the payload. Anyone can read it.
Trusting claims without verifying the signature.
Ignoring exp and aud. An expired token that never expires is a gift to an attacker.
Accepting the algorithm from the token itself. Always pin the expected alg on the server side.
Can anyone read a JWT? Yes. The header and payload are encoded, not encrypted.
Does decoding prove the token is valid? No. Validity comes from signature and claim verification.
Is my token uploaded when I inspect it? It should not be. Some online decoders send the token to a server, which is a bad idea for a credential — decoding can happen entirely in the browser.
If you need to eyeball a token quickly, I built a free JWT Decoder that runs entirely client-side, so nothing leaves your browser. (It is my own project — the explanation above stands on its own.)

articles.title: GRC Analyst Explained
articles.description:
Cybersecurity is often pictured as a world of hoodie-clad hackers and blinking terminal screens, but a huge part of keeping organizations safe actually happens away from the code. It happens in policy documents, audit rooms, and risk registers. The person behind that work is the GRC analyst, and this role has quietly become one of the more dependable and well-paying entry points into the broader security field. If you have never heard the term before, or only know it in passing, here is a full picture of what the job actually involves and why so many people are moving toward it.
Part of the appeal is that this role does not depend on any one industry. Banks need GRC analysts to satisfy financial regulators. Hospitals need them to protect patient data under health privacy laws. 
Software companies need them to pass the security reviews that enterprise customers demand before signing a contract. Wherever there is data, regulation, or reputational risk, there is a place for someone to manage governance, risk, and compliance in a structured way.
GRC stands for Governance, Risk, and Compliance, three pillars that together decide how safely and legally a business operates. Governance covers the policies and decision-making structures a company follows. Risk covers everything that could threaten the business, from a data breach to a missed regulatory deadline. Compliance covers whether the company is actually meeting the laws, contracts, and industry standards it is bound by.
A GRC analyst sits at the center of these three areas, monitoring risk, documenting controls, and making sure the business can prove it is doing what it says it is doing when an auditor or regulator comes knocking. For readers who want a deeper technical walkthrough of the position, including tools and daily workflows, this breakdown of the GRC analyst role in cybersecurity is worth a read.
No two days look exactly the same, but a typical week usually involves a mix of the following:
Regulations are not slowing down. Every year brings updated privacy laws, new industry standards, and stricter expectations from customers and investors about how data is handled. A company that cannot prove its compliance posture risks fines, lost contracts, and reputational damage that can take years to repair. This has pushed GRC from a background administrative function into something closer to a strategic necessity, sitting right next to security operations and legal in terms of importance.
It also helps that GRC work does not require the same steep technical ramp-up as roles like penetration testing or security engineering. People coming from audit, legal, IT support, or even project management backgrounds often transition into GRC roles successfully because the underlying skills of documentation, structured thinking, and stakeholder communication already transfer well.
If this career path sounds appealing, here is what tends to matter most to employers:
Certifications carry real influence in this field. CompTIA Security+ is a common starting point for those new to security concepts, while CRISC, CISA, and CISM are widely recognized once you are ready to specialize further in risk, audit, or leadership tracks.
Soft skills matter just as much as technical ones in this line of work. A GRC analyst regularly has to explain to a non-technical executive why a particular risk matters, or convince a busy engineering team to prioritize a fix that has no visible impact on the product itself. Being able to translate risk into business consequences, calmly and clearly, is often what separates a good GRC analyst from a great one.
Most people enter the field as a junior GRC analyst or compliance associate, spending their first year or two learning frameworks and supporting audits. From there, the path usually leads to a full GRC analyst role, then senior GRC analyst, and eventually GRC manager or compliance director. Some professionals use this as a stepping stone toward broader security leadership positions, including Chief Information Security Officer, particularly if they build strong relationships across security, legal, and executive teams along the way.
Pay tends to climb steadily with each certification and additional year of ownership over a framework or audit relationship. It is also one of the more remote-friendly corners of cybersecurity, since the bulk of the work is documentation, assessment, and collaboration rather than physical or on-site tasks.
One underrated benefit of this career track is how transferable it is across industries once you have built a solid foundation. A GRC analyst who has spent a few years working with ISO 27001 and SOC 2 in a technology company can usually move into a similar role at a healthcare or financial services organization without starting from scratch, since the core skills of risk assessment, control documentation, and audit readiness carry over even as the specific regulations change.
The sheer number of frameworks, acronyms, and certifications in this space can feel intimidating at first. The trick is to pick one framework, learn it properly, and build outward from there rather than trying to absorb everything at once. Pairing that focused learning with a beginner-friendly security certification and some hands-on practice with a GRC tool is usually enough to make a compelling case to employers looking for junior talent.
For anyone comparing GRC against other cybersecurity specializations before committing to a learning path, Thinkcloudly's library of cybersecurity career guides is a useful place to compare roles side by side before deciding where to focus.
The GRC analyst role rarely gets the same attention as flashier cybersecurity titles, but it plays a genuinely essential part in keeping organizations both safe and compliant. It rewards people who like structure, clear communication, and connecting the dots between policy and real-world risk. For anyone looking for a stable, well-respected way into cybersecurity that does not require years of hands-on hacking experience, this is one of the more practical and future-proof paths available today.

articles.title: どうやって Claude Code と開発してる？ ― いまの回し方をまるごと書き出してみた
articles.description:
はじめに
#
Claude Code を利用した個人開発の進め方が、最近一定の形に落ち着いてきました。
何度も作り変えてきたので、いまの形も通過点だと思います。それでも「どうやって Claude Code と開発してるんですか？」と聞かれたときに渡せるものとして、現状の構造をひととおり書き出しておきます。
 -->
 Information
この記事は「こう作るべき」という提案ではありません。あくまで、ぼくはこう回しているという記録です。
この記事の構成
#
本記事の構成は以下の通りです。
全体像：開発サイクル全体を1枚の図で示し、読み方を説明します
このプロジェクトの憲法：図の前提になっている「何をどこに書き残すか」「どう守らせるか」「どこで人間が判断するか」という3つのルールを説明します
【第1部】1つの機能ができるまで：Plan → TDD → Review → Verify → Commit → CI という実際の1サイクルを、4つの Gate と合わせて左から順に追います
【第2部】どの情報を、どこに置いているか：ルール・スキル・サブエージェント・スクリプトなどに何を書き、なぜそこに置いたのかを書きます
おわりに：いまの形が通過点であることと、まだ答えが出ていない課題を書きます
全体の設計だけ知りたければ最初の2章、実際の運用フローまで知りたければ第1部まで、資材の置き方まで踏み込みたければ第2部まで読んでもらえれば幸いです。
全体像
#
まず1枚で。これがいま回っているものの全体です。

この図の読み方は以下の通りです。
上の枠が材料です。開発中に人間や Claude Code が繰り返し読むドキュメントで、docs/adr/ や .claude/rules/ 等々が並んでいます
下の枠が実行です。01 Plan から 06 CI まで、左から右に時間が流れます

05 Commit までは手元の環境、06 CI から先は GitHub Actions です。実行環境が変わるので、色を変えて破線で区切ってあります
黒い菱形 A〜D は、ぼくが判断する場所です
マゼンタの docs/adr/ / criteria.yaml は上下に2つありますが、これは同じものです。判断や指摘が記録され、それが次の開発サイクルの材料に戻ります
この記事では、この図を左から順に追ったあと、図には描けなかった部分を詳解していきます。
このプロジェクトの憲法
#
図の前提になっているルールが3つあります。
ルール
概要




行き先を決めてから、書き残す
4段階のふるいで ADR / コード / 設計書 / 書かない に振り分ける


書いて守らせるのではなく、書けなくする
型で表現不能にすることを最優先にする


ぼくが判断する場面を決めておく
判断を引き取る場所を工程の中に4箇所固定する




行き先を決めてから、書き残す
#
実装していると、コードの外に書き残しておきたいことが次々に出てきます。「なぜこの方式を選んだか」「全体はどう噛み合っているか」「この値の上限はいくつか」「デプロイはどう回すか」等々です。
以前はこれを片っ端から設計書に足していました。その結果、認証まわりの設計書が 3,000 行を超えたあたりでコードと設計書の内容が食い違いはじめます。どちらが正しいのか分からない。直すには2箇所を直さないといけない。そのうち設計書のほうを見なくなる。
そこで、書き残したいことが出てきたら先に置き場所を決めるようにしました。役割ごとの媒体はこうです。
役割
媒体




WHAT（何を作るか）
要件定義書


WHY（なぜそう作るか）
ADR


HOW（どう作るか）
ソースコード（型・関数・zod schema）


VERIFY（正しく作られたか）
テストコード


OVERVIEW（俯瞰・統合）
設計書



ただしこの表だけでは決まりません。たとえば「エラー処理はミドルウェアで一元化する」という内容は、そう決めた理由（WHY）でもあり、全体構成の一部（OVERVIEW）でもあります。同じ内容が ADR にも設計書にも行けてしまいます。
分かれ目を、決定を1つ切り取るか、全体の整合を1枚にまとめるかに設定しました。ADR は決定するたびに1ファイル増えるので、いま 124 本あります。設計書は「全体構成」「デプロイ手順」のように枚数が決まっていて、決定が増えると中身が追従します。
「この方式を選んだ理由」なら ADR、「全体がどう噛み合っているか」なら設計書へという具合です。
そのうえで、書き残したい内容ごとに4つの問いを上から順にかけて、最初に YES が出た行き先へ書き残したいことを送ります。
問い
YES の行き先




Q1. それは「決定」か？（代替案・トレードオフがある）
ADR（1決定1ファイル）


Q2. コード / 型 / テスト / OpenAPI を読めば再生成できる事実か？
コードが真正ソース。ドキュメントには参照だけ残す


Q3. コードが変わるたびに変わる（揮発する）か？
ドキュメントには書かない。コード側に持たせるか、コードから自動生成する


Q4. 安定 ∧ コードの単一箇所から不可視か？
設計書の領分



冒頭に挙げた4つを、この表に通してみます。「なぜこの方式を選んだか」は Q1 で ADR へ。「この値の上限はいくつか」は Q2 でコードへ。「全体はどう噛み合っているか」と「デプロイはどう回すか」は Q4 で設計書へ行きます。
この4つの問いで振り分けると、Q4 まで生き残るのは下記4類型と整理できました。
統合俯瞰（全体構成図）
横断の流儀（命名やログ項目の標準）
運用知識（デプロイ手順・runbook）
ドメイン言語（用語集・コンテキストマップ）
いずれも「数ヶ月・多ファイルをまたいで真であり続ける」かつ「コードの1箇所を読んでも見えない」の交差領域です。
結果として、詳細設計書は書きません。ここでいう詳細設計書は、コードを書く前にクラス構成・関数のシグネチャ・項目定義・バリデーション規則・処理シーケンスを文章で決めておく、ウォーターフォールでいう「詳細設計」工程の成果物です。シグネチャや項目定義は型を読めば再生成できるので Q2 で、クラス構成や処理シーケンスはコードが変わるたびに変わるので Q3 で落ちます。
書いて守らせるのではなく、書けなくする
#
規約を守らせる手段はいくつかありますが、いちばん優先するのは「型で表現不能にする」ことと決めています。ドキュメントに「こうしてください」と書いて守らせるのではなく、違反そのものを起こせなくする。
実際にそうしている箇所を2つ挙げます。
ID の偽造を、型と lint で禁止する
ユーザー ID のような識別子は、ただの string ではなく branded type にしています。
export const UserIdSchema = z
  .string()
  .min(1)
  .max(128)
  .regex(/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$/)
  .brand<"UserId">();

export type UserId = z.infer<typeof UserIdSchema>;

export const userId = (raw: string): UserId =>
  enforceInvariant(UserIdSchema, raw, "UserId");


  

.brand<"UserId">() が付いているので、生の string を UserId 型の引数に渡すとコンパイルエラーになります。UserId を作るには userId() を通すしかなく、そこで長さと文字種の検証が走ります。検証を通っていない値は、型のうえで存在できません。
ただし、型には抜け道があります。"anything" as UserId とキャストすれば、検証を通さずに UserId 型を名乗れます。
// eslint.config.mjs
const noAsBrandedScalarVo = {
  selector:
    "TSAsExpression[typeAnnotation.typeName.name=/^(UserId|BudgetId|SpendingQuadrant|BudgetQuadrant)$/]",
  message:
    "branded scalar / 列挙 VO への as キャストは型偽造の抜け道。生成は VO の factory 経由のみ。",
};


  

as UserId と書いた時点で lint が落ちます。「ID は必ず userId() で作ってください」とドキュメントに書く代わりに、型で塞ぎ、型の抜け道を lint で塞いでいます。
対応表の書き漏れを、コンパイルエラーにする
literal union で定義した値ごとに、対応する値を紐づける。こういう対応表をいくつか使っています。
type Status = "todo" | "doing" | "done";

const STATUS_SLUG = {
  todo: "to-do",
  doing: "in-progress",
  done: "done",
} as const satisfies Record<Status, string>;


  

末尾の satisfies Record<Status, string> により、union の全メンバーが揃っていないと型エラーになります。Status にメンバーを1つ足した瞬間、この表の更新漏れがビルド時に落ちます。レビューで気づく必要がありません。
どちらも共通しているのは、守られたかどうかを人間が確認していないことです。違反したらコンパイルか lint で落ちて、レビューまで届きません。
ぼくが判断する場面を決めておく
#
規約と型で縛っても、実装中には必ず判断の要る場面が出てきます。そこでぼくが判断を引き取る場所を工程の中に4箇所配置しました。
Gate
ぼくが判断すること




A
承認済みテストケースを変えるかどうか


B
実装中に発覚した設計方針をどう変えるか


C
重大なレビュー指摘を、いま直すか先送りするか


D
既存の ADR と現実のコードが食い違ったときの解釈





【第1部】1つの機能ができるまで
#
この章では、1つの機能を作る間に前章の3つのルールがどう働くかを追っていきます。
Plan → TDD → Review → Verify → Commit → CI
       A B     C                 D


  

チェーンの下の A〜D が Gate の位置です。TDD で2回、Review と Commit で1回ずつ、判断がぼくに戻ってきます。
各工程の手順は feature-implementation スキルにまとめてあり、Claude Code は最初のファイルを書く前にこれを読み込みます。
1. 計画する
#
まず、これから触る領域に関係する ADR を Claude Code に読ませます。とはいえ 124 本(現時点の数値)あるので、毎回全部渡すわけにはいきません。そこで CLAUDE.md に索引を持っています。
触る領域
必読 ADR
関連設計書




認証 / 認可
0030, 0031, 0032, 0042
authentication-design.md


ロギング / 監査ログ
0009, 0033 §1.3, 0037 §3, 0042
logging-monitoring.md


Hono ミドルウェア
0037, 0038
middleware-architecture.md


エラー戦略
0035, 0041, 0042, 0043, 0045, 0047
error-handling-architecture.md



Claude Code は着手前にこの表を引いて、該当する ADR だけを読みます。
次に、馴染みのない領域なら Explore エージェントで前例を探します。これは「既存の実装パターンを探す」ためのもので、狙いは実装の不整合を防ぐことです。
たとえば新しく xxxConfig.ts を作ろうとしたとき、すでに authConfig.ts が同じ構造で存在しているなら、それに倣うべきです。
3ファイル以上に触る、アーキテクチャを変える、あるいは前例を探したら食い違うものが2つ出てきた。このどれかなら、さらに Plan エージェントを挟みます。
計画は、Plan エージェントを使ったかどうかに関わらず、.claude/docs/plan/ にスナップショットとして保存します。
このスナップショットは陳腐化する前提で置いています。実装が進めば計画とはズレるので、最新に保つ努力はしません。「当時どう段取りしたか」の記録として残すだけです。ここを「常に正しく保つドキュメント」にしようとすると、また二重管理が始まります。
なお、Explore と Plan は Claude Code に組み込まれているエージェントで、このプロジェクトで定義したものではありません。
 -->
 Information
Explore と Plan を呼ぶ条件を上記のように資材へ明記していますが、エージェントが毎回この通りに動くわけではありません。条件に当てはまっているのに Explore を飛ばして書き始める、ということは普通に起きます。ここに書いているのは「そう指示している」であって、「必ずそうなる」ではありません。
2. テストから書く
#
テストの書き方はルールファイル testing.md が持っていて、エージェントはそれに従います。
Always follow a two-phase approach: define test cases → review → implement. Never implement tests before the user approves the test case list.
空のテストケースだけを先に書いて、ぼくにレビューを出す手順です。実際にはこういうものが提示されます。
describe("BudgetAmount", () => {
  // 正常系
  test("正の整数から生成できる", () => {});
  test("上限値ちょうどは生成できる", () => {});

  // 異常系
  test("0 以下は生成できない", () => {});
  test("上限を超える額は生成できない", () => {});
  test("小数を含む値は生成できない", () => {});

  // 境界
  test("上限 + 1 は生成できない", () => {});
});


  

中身は空で、test の説明文だけがある状態です。この状態で「この観点で合っていますか」と聞かれます。
ここで承認したテストケースをあとから変更するには、ぼくの承認が要ります。これが Gate A です。

  Gate D の実例
ADR には「エラー処理は errorMiddleware で行う」と書いてありました。リクエスト処理の途中に挟むミドルウェアで、ハンドラが投げた例外を捕まえる想定です。ところが実装してみると、バックエンドに使っている Hono では、ミドルウェアの中で try/catch してもハンドラの例外を捕まえられませんでした。フレームワークが内部で例外を処理してしまうためです。捕まえるには、Hono が用意している app.onError() という別の登録口を使う必要がありました。
ここで ADR の「errorMiddleware」を「app.onError のことだ」と読み替えて進めることもできます。ただそれをやると、実装に存在しない仕組みが ADR に書かれたまま残ります。そこで新しい ADR を書いて、この技術制約と、以降は「errorMiddleware」を app.onError のハンドラとして読む、という解釈を残しました。元の ADR の本文は書き換えていません。

第1部に出てきた Review 工程で feedback-reviewer が照らす「観点」は、.claude/feedback/criteria.yaml という観点表にあります。
- id: corrections:260816-115935-1
  pattern: 変更した用語・値・コマンド・手順を、同じものを記述する他資材（他 ADR / plan / CLAUDE.md / rules / 設定ファイル）へ波及させず、旧記述を残したまま提示する
  scope: docs/**/*.md, .claude/**/*.md, CLAUDE.md
  detection_hint: 差分で置き換えた用語・数値・コマンド文字列を rg でリポジトリ全体に検索し、ヒットした他ファイルが同じ差分に含まれているかを照合する
  occurrence: 10


  

ぼくの発言が観点表の項目になり、レビューで使われ、役目を終えて消えるまでの流れはこうです。

feedback-distiller エージェントが蓄積された発言を読み、矯正にあたるものを抽出して、既存の項目と同種かを分類する
昇格候補をぼくに提示し、承認した分だけ観点表に書く
feedback-reviewer が、Review 工程でコード差分を観点表に照らす
何度照らしても違反が見つからない項目は、feedback-prune フックが観点表から落とす。
なお、この蒸留は開発サイクルの中では回しません。
feedback-nudge フックが未蒸留の発言があると知らせてきたときにまとめて回しています。
ADR や規約が「決めたこと」を残す仕組みだとすると、こちらは「言ったのに守られなかったこと」を残す仕組みです。
おわりに
#
はじめにで書いたとおり、この形も通過点だと思います。実際、第1部で書いた Gate は、この記事を書いている間に見直しました。
ほかにも、まだ答えが出ていないことがあります。
ぼくがタスクのボトルネックになっている：いまは勉強の意味も込めて、成果物に全部目を通しています。そのぶん、タスクがぼくのところで止まります。
チームで開発するときの仕組みがない：ここまでの仕組みは、ぼく1人での開発を前提に作っています。複数人で一緒に開発する場面での仕組みは、まだ整えられていないと感じています。
要求から実装までが、ひと続きになっていない：この記事で書いたのは、要件が決まったあとの開発プロセスです。その上流で顧客の要望・要求を整理して開発の要件に落とし込み、設計して実装するまでを通しでつなぐ仕組みは、まだ整備できていないと感じています。
どれもすぐに答えが出るものではないので、今後も自分で試行錯誤しながら、少しずつ整備していきたいと思います。

articles.title: Connecting Claude and Other LLMs to a Custom .NET MCP Server – A Production‑Ready Guide
articles.description:
Quick Answer


connecting Claude and other LLMs to a custom .NET MCP server: Learn how to architect, secure, and optimize a custom .NET MCP server for Claude, Azure OpenAI, and other LLMs. Real‑world code, performance tricks, and production pitfalls included.
When you bolt Claude, GPT‑4 or any other LLM straight into a .NET endpoint, the first 200 requests look great. But as soon as you hit a few hundred concurrent users, you start seeing a cascade of symptoms: 200‑plus millisecond latency, sporadic 429s, cache pollution, and a brittle tool‑calling pipeline that breaks on the slightest provider change. The root cause is that most quick‑starts treat the LLM as a black‑box HTTP call and ignore the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the contract that lets you swap providers, reuse KV caches, and enforce tenant isolation without touching business logic.
Consider a SaaS company that offers a knowledge‑base chatbot to its customers. They ship a minimal API that forwards every user query to Claude. Within a week the product is used by 12,000 concurrent sessions. Suddenly the team sees:
Average response latency jumps from 800 ms to 3.2 s.
Rate‑limit errors from Claude surface 12% of the time.
Tenant A receives answers that belong to Tenant B.
Tool calls (e.g., SQL lookup) start timing out because the adapter no longer preserves the tenantId in the cache key.
Under the hood, the API was a simple wrapper around ClaudeClient.ChatAsync and a naive MemoryCache. There was no MCP layer, no unified tool registry, no observability, and no failover strategy. The result: a production system that can’t scale, is insecure, and is hard to debug.
Protocol‑agnostic vs. provider‑specific optimisations  
Pros of MCP: One codebase for all LLMs, centralised caching, consistent observability, easier compliance checks.


Cons: You lose provider‑level tuning knobs (e.g., Claude’s parallel_requests or Azure-ai-foundry-vs-azure-openai-service-observability-in-production-20261007" class="internal-link">Azure’s function_call Semantics) unless you expose them in the MCP schema. Adding a new field means updating every adapter and potentially breaking existing deployments.
Centralised cache vs. distributed cache  
Pros: A single Redis cluster simplifies key design and eviction policies.


Cons: Network latency to Redis can dominate inference time if the cluster is in a different region. A per‑tenant cache shard can mitigate this but increases operational complexity.
Strict tenant isolation vs. performance  
Pros: Prefixing keys with {tenantId}: guarantees no cross‑tenant leakage.


Cons: It reduces cache hit rates for shared system prompts. A shared cache with a deterministic hash of the system prompt and tenant ID can mitigate but requires careful key design.
Use the following matrix to decide whether to adopt a custom MCP Server or stick with provider SDKs.



Criterion
Custom MCP
Provider SDK




Multi‑tenant isolation required
✓
✗


Need to switch providers at runtime
✓
✗


Observability across providers
✓
✗


Latency budget < 1 s
✓ (with careful caching)
✓ (but no cache reuse)


Operational overhead acceptable
✓
✗ (less code but more provider lock‑in)



In most SaaS or enterprise scenarios, the benefits of a MCP Server outweigh the extra operational burden.
Even with a well‑designed MCP Server, you can hit failure modes:
Cache stampede – If many tenants hit a cache miss for the same system prompt, the server will flood the LLM backend. Mitigate with LazyCache or a SemaphoreSlim per key.
Provider drift – When a provider updates its API (e.g., Claude adds a new field), the adapter can silently break. Implement a versioned MCP schema and a health‑check that validates adapter compatibility.
Back‑pressure misconfiguration – A bounded channel that’s too small will drop requests under load; too large will consume memory. Tune the channel size based on observed QPS and average inference latency.
Security mis‑configuration – If tenant isolation is disabled or the API key is leaked to a malicious tenant, the KV cache can be read or corrupted. Use Azure AD scopes that map 1 to tenant IDs and enforce them in every request.
Ignoring the Metadata bag – Developers often forget to propagate tenant IDs into the adapter, leading to cross‑tenant cache pollution.
Hard‑coding system prompts – Embedding the system prompt in code means every provider change requires a redeploy. Store system prompts in a shared KV store and reference them by hash.
Over‑caching the entire conversation – Caching the full chat history can quickly exhaust Redis memory. Cache only the last N tokens or the prompt + first assistant message.
Not handling provider rate limits – A 429 from Claude is treated as a fatal error. Implement back‑off and a fallback policy (e.g., switch to Claude Instant).
Missing observability hooks – Without tracing at the adapter level, you can’t correlate latency spikes to specific providers or tool calls.
In a recent production rollout for a financial services firm, we adopted the following pattern that cut latency by 35% and eliminated cross‑tenant leaks:
Use RedisCache with HashTags to group keys by tenant. The key format is {tenantId}:prompt:{hash} and the hash is a SHA‑256 of the concatenated system prompt + user message.
Implement a RequestQueue that is a bounded Channel<McpChatRequest> with a back‑pressure strategy that returns HTTP 429 when full.
Expose a ProviderRegistry that maps provider names to adapters and includes a HealthCheck endpoint that pings each adapter’s /health route. If a provider is unhealthy, the registry marks it as degraded and routes traffic to a fallback provider.
Instrument the MCP server with OpenTelemetry, exporting traces to Azure Monitor. Use span.SetAttribute("provider") and span.SetAttribute("tenant") to filter dashboards by tenant.
For tool execution, use a ToolExecutorFactory that lazily loads executors from a DI container. This keeps the startup footprint small and allows adding new tools without redeploying the MCP server.
Deploy the MCP server as a stateless container in Azure Container Apps with a scale‑out rule based on CPU% > 70% and QPS > 200. Use a sidecar Redis instance in the same subnet to reduce network hops.
Inference latency – The adapter adds ~5 ms overhead. Cache hits reduce token count by 15–25%, cutting provider cost per request.
Throughput – With a 30 ms per request average, a single container can handle ~3k QPS. Scale horizontally by adding more replicas; use Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler with custom metrics.
Cache hit ratio – A 70% hit ratio on the KV cache keeps token usage low. Monitor CacheHitRate in Redis and adjust TTLs accordingly.
Network hops – Keep the MCP server, Redis, and LLM provider in the same region to avoid 200–300 ms round‑trips. If you must cross regions, use Azure Front Door to route traffic and reduce latency.
When scaling a MCP server, remember:
Statelessness – All state must be external (Redis, blob storage). This allows the autoscaler to spin up new instances without losing context.
Connection pooling – Use HttpClientFactory to pool connections to LLM providers. Disable KeepAlive for providers that don’t support it to avoid socket exhaustion.
Graceful shutdown – Implement IHostedService.StopAsync that drains the request queue before terminating. This prevents orphaned requests that never hit the LLM backend.
Observability – Expose a /metrics endpoint for Prometheus. Include metrics for request_latency_seconds, cache_hit_rate, provider_errors_total, and tenant_requests_total.
Cost control – Use Azure Cost Management to set alerts on token usage. Combine this with a RateLimiter that caps requests per tenant to avoid runaway costs.
Expose a single, unified /chat REST endpoint that accepts a JSON body with model, prompt, temperature, max_tokens and returns a standardized JSON response containing content, usage, provider, and cost_estimate.
Implement a provider‑router that maps the model field to the corresponding provider SDK via a shared interface, and add a fallback path to an alternative provider when the primary returns an error or times out.
Add per‑request cost estimation headers (e.g., X-Estimated-Cost) derived from live provider pricing tables, and emit provider‑specific latency metrics to your observability stack (Prometheus/CloudWatch).
Integrate a circuit‑breaker that trips after three consecutive failures for a provider, temporarily redirecting traffic to a safe fallback or returning a 503 with a Retry-After header.
Store all prompt templates in a versioned, cache‑able repository; load them at startup and expose a /prompts/{name} endpoint that returns the current template and its hash to detect drift.
Deploy a feature‑flag (e.g., LaunchDarkly, Split.io) that toggles between the custom MCP implementation and the provider SDK directly, enabling controlled roll‑outs and instant rollback if issues surface.
Connecting Claude and other LLMs to a custom .NET MCP server is not a novelty; it’s a maturity step that turns a brittle prototype into a production‑grade platform. The trade‑offs are clear: you pay operational overhead for a unified protocol, but you gain tenant isolation, observability, and the flexibility to orchestrate multiple providers. By following the patterns above—centralised adapters, bounded queues, tenant‑aware caching, and a robust observability stack—you can build a system that scales, stays secure, and remains maintainable even as you add new LLMs, tool calls, or vector database integrations.
