articles.title: GitOS: Graph-Powered Ecosystem Defense & Intelligence Layer for GitHub
articles.description:
Why We Built GitOS: The Graph-Powered Defense Layer Open Source Desperately Needs


By Naimish Singh & Team BitBuddies (Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents 2026)
If you maintain an open-source library with more than a few hundred stars, you already know what happened over the last twelve months:
Your notifications exploded. But they didn’t explode with deep bug reports or thoughtful refactors. They exploded with AI-generated pull requests.
Someone pastes an issue into a frontier LLM, prompts it to "fix this," and hits Submit PR without reading a single line of the diff. On the surface, the PR looks articulate. The markdown description is immaculate, formatted with bullet points and emojis. But when you inspect the code:
Variable names were renamed cosmetically across 18 files.
A modified helper function in routing.py broke 14 callers across unrelated modules because the author never ran the test suite.
A newly hallucinated utility function was injected into the codebase that is never called by anything (in_degree == 0).
Worse: existing automated "AI review bots" chime in by generating 50-comment threads, burning tens of thousands of LLM tokens on speculative guesses while spamming everyone on the thread.
We watched maintainers of projects like FastAPI, Flask, and React spend their weekends acting as human spam filters. 
We asked ourselves a simple engineering question:
Why are we using stochastic, token-hungry LLMs to guess at structural code relationships when a graph database can determine them with 100% mathematical certainty in under 10 milliseconds?
That question gave birth to GitOS.
Before building GitOS, we laid down three non-negotiable architectural axioms:
Zero LLM Tokens for Structural Math: An LLM should never be asked "what functions call add_api_route?" That is a graph traversal problem.
Zero Disk Clone: Open-source maintainers don’t want a bot cloning 5GB repositories to a third-party server. Everything must parse directly from GitHub’s recursive Git Trees API in-memory.
Zero Unconsented Bot Spam: No automated comments, labels, or PR closures unless a human maintainer clicks a button with an explicit confirmation dialog under their own authenticated OAuth session.
To make this possible, we needed a graph engine with sub-millisecond traversal latencies on in-memory topologies. That engine was FalkorDB.
When a maintainer or contributor pastes a GitHub PR URL into GitOS, the system doesn’t prompt an LLM. Instead, it triggers a 4-layer deterministic pipeline:
[GitHub PR URL] 
      │
      ▼ (In-Memory Tree Fetch - 0 Disk Clones)
[Universal AST Parser (Python & Tree-Sitter)]
      │
      ▼ (Subgraphs Persisted by commit_sha)
[(FalkorDB Graph Engine)]
      │
      ├──> Filter 1: Untested Call-Graph Impact ([:TESTED_BY] Traversal)
      ├──> Filter 2: AST Delta vs. Raw Text Diff Ratio (Cosmetic Churn)
      ├──> Filter 3: Dead Code Injection (In-Degree == 0)
      └──> Filter 4: Maintainer Architectural Boundaries (Forbidden Edges)
      │
      ▼ (Sub-10ms Subgraph Results)
[3D Interactive Force Graph & Multi-Agent Swarm]

We extract classes, functions, calls, and imports into formal graph primitives:
Nodes: (:Function), (:Class), (:Module), (:Test)

Relationships: [:CALLS], [:IMPORTS], [:TESTED_BY], [:DEFINES]




  
  
  2. The FalkorDB Cypher Queries Doing the Heavy Lifting


Instead of asking an AI to "spot bugs", GitOS executes deterministic Cypher queries directly against FalkorDB.
A. Multi-Hop Blast Radius:
MATCH (target:Function) WHERE target.id IN $modified_targets
MATCH path = (caller:Function)-[:CALLS*1..$hops]->(target)
RETURN caller.id, target.id, length(path) AS hop_distance
ORDER BY hop_distance ASC LIMIT 100;

In FalkorDB, this recursive traversal returns in 3 to 7 milliseconds. It instantly reveals that changing APIRouter.add_api_route in Python cascades into an unverified TypeScript gateway controller two hops away.
B. Catching Hallucinated Dead Code:
MATCH (fn:Function {commit_sha: $commit_sha})
WHERE NOT fn.name STARTS WITH 'test_' AND NOT fn.name STARTS WITH '__'
OPTIONAL MATCH (caller:Function)-[:CALLS]->(fn)
WITH fn, count(caller) AS in_degree
WHERE in_degree = 0
RETURN fn.id, fn.file_path, fn.line_start;

If in_degree == 0, GitOS immediately flags the injected symbol as potential AI hallucination. Zero tokens spent.
C. Cosmetic Churn Ratio:
Only after FalkorDB computes the deterministic metrics does our 5-agent swarm take the stage:
TriageAgent: Synthesizes the blast radius score and maintainer executive brief.
GraphAgent: Traverses isolated repository graphs (gitos_{owner}_{repo}) to identify cross-module dependency regressions.
SecurityAgent: Scans for AST security sinks (eval, command injection) and package slopsquatting.
OnboardingAgent & Pathfinder: Translates open GitHub issues into precise AST symbol edit scopes for contributors.
ReleaseAgent: Analyzes AST changes to automatically determine semantic SemVer impacts (PATCH, MINOR, or MAJOR) and draft structured release notes.
Because FalkorDB compresses the entire problem into a tiny, high-density subgraph, when we do call an LLM (Groq Llama 3.3 70B), the prompt is under 800 tokens. No prompt bloat, no token bankruptcy, and no hallucinations.
When we started the hackathon, we experimented with relational joins and document stores. They fell apart the moment we hit multi-hop traversals across enterprise codebases like Flask and FastAPI.
With FalkorDB:
Speed is real: Running recursive graph traversals on Redis-backed memory primitives gave our agents sub-second responsiveness on live UI keystrokes.
Multi-Graph Isolation is a superpower: FalkorDB lets you create isolated graphs (gitos_fastapi_fastapi, gitos_pallets_flask) on the fly inside a single instance without deploying separate database clusters. This made multi-tenant per-repo memory effortless.
Traceability replaces guesswork: In an era where AI agents are accused of being black boxes, a Cypher query path (A)-[:CALLS]->(B)-[:CALLS]->(C) is deterministic proof you can show to any senior engineer.
We made sure anyone—especially hackathon judges—can run GitOS locally with a single command:
git clone https://github.com/ace-ify/GitOS.git
cd GitOS
cp .env.example .env
# Add your GitHub token in .env
docker-compose up --build

Open http://localhost:3000 to interact with the 3D topology graph.
API Swagger docs live at http://localhost:8000/docs.
Test suite: 40/40 unit & integration tests passing out of the box.
AI shouldn’t make open source harder to maintain. It should make ecosystems cleaner, safer, and more accessible.
By pairing modern AI agents with the structural rigor of FalkorDB graph databases, we don't just guess what code does—we trace it, defend it, and understand it.
Check out the open-source code on GitHub: https://github.com/ace-ify/GitOS

articles.title: Gemma 4 reads, code decides: offline NDIS invoicing that caught 20 of 22 restraints
articles.description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle
Sunday night in Melbourne. Mel has four participants and a phone full of notes like this:
Tues (Cup day!!) - Jake 3 till 8:30ish. Footy training then tea at his place.
Locked the pantry so he would stop snacking before dinner, he was pretty upset about it.


Mel is not a real person; she is a composite from published rate guides and NDIS Commission material. BUt the job is real: an independent NDIS support worker on an ABN, unpaid for the hours it takes to turn that diary into invoices. That line holds two traps.
The price. Melbourne Cup Day is a public holiday in Melbourne and most of Victoria, and in no other state, so all 5.5 hours go on the public-holiday item at $163.46 an hour, not the weekday $73.58. On an ordinary Tuesday the shift crosses 8pm and the whole support takes the higher rate; splitting at 8pm underclaims.

The pantry. Locking a pantry to stop someone snacking is an environmental restraint under the NDIS (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018. For a registered provider, unauthorised use is a reportable incident: 5 business days to notify the NDIS Commission, 24 hours if it caused harm. An unregistered sole trader like Mel may not use one at all, and the Commission asks for it to be raised with them. Either way it reads like an ordinary note; Mel would have invoiced it and moved on.

Arvo does the Sunday-night job and asks the awkward question. Type, photograph or dictate the week; get back invoice lines a plan manager will accept, a printable invoice per participant, a CSV, and a red flag quoting the exact sentence with a notify-by date. Gemma 4 runs through Ollama on the worker's laptop; nothing is sent anywhere.
Who pays. Independent ABN support workers, at a proposed $12 a month or $99 a year. The platforms that already do NDIS invoicing are priced for agencies: ShiftCare charges per user and says "All plans start at a minimum of five staff". Her alternative is a spreadsheet and an unbilled hour.
  
  


Live demo page (a saved real run, no install): https://otto-deviant1904.github.io/arvo/

13.6 seconds from button to invoices (the wait is sped up; the button's counter is real).
The page is docs/demo/run.json rendered: gemma4:e4b on docs/demo/diary.txt, 7 shifts, 10 invoice lines, 3 flags, 13.3 seconds on a laptop RTX 4050 (6 GB). Your own diary: ollama pull gemma4:e4b (6.6 GB), clone, python -m arvo serve. Python 3.12 standard library, nothing else.

That week is all right, and I had seen it while building; the held-out numbers are below.
Then I tried it on real handwriting. I copied one of the test weeks onto lined paper in my own writing, photographed it with my phone and ran it once. Gemma 4 did far worse than on the rendered test photos: 0 of 7 shifts fully right. It got every date and most times, but it read my "Jake" as "Jane" and my "Tom" as "7om", so 6 of 7 shifts matched nobody on the roster; my "km" reads as "pm", so every distance was lost; and "Thurs - nothing on" became an empty shift. What held: every one of those shifts came back with a check, the unmatched names were never priced, and the garage note was still flagged as seclusion. On my handwriting Arvo is a first draft for a human to fix, not an invoice.

And from voice memos recorded in the car. Gemma 4 hears the audio itself, no separate speech model. Here it read "half 11" as 10:30, and the check after the fix put it back to 11:30 and told the worker why.

 / 
        arvo
      
    

Arvo
Sunday-night invoicing for NDIS support workers, on a laptop, with nothing sent anywhere.
An independent (ABN) NDIS support worker in Victoria types, photographs or dictates their week of shifts the way they actually write them:
Tues (Cup day!!) - Jake 3 till 8:30ish. Footy training then tea at his place
Locked the pantry so he would stop snacking before dinner, he was pretty upset about it.


Arvo gives back:
Invoice lines a plan manager will accept. Support item number, date, hours, rate and total for every shift, priced by code against the official NDIS Pricing Schedule 2026-27 and the Victorian public-holiday calendar. That shift is on Melbourne Cup Day, so the whole 5.5 hours goes on 04_102_0125_6_1 at $163.46/h. The same shift on an ordinary Tuesday crosses 8pm, so all of it is claimed at the evening rate, not split (Schedule s2.4(c)).
A red flag for the sentence that…

  
View on GitHub
MIT. One shape:
diary text ─┐
photo ──────┼─> Gemma 4 reads ─> shifts (who, date, start, end, km) ─> code checks fields against the diary
voice memo ─┘                                                                      │
        invoice lines, printable invoice, CSV <─ pricing from the official JSON <──┘
                                                 (band, Vic holiday, s2.4(c), item number)

each note ─> Gemma 4 reads ─> possible restrictive practice ─> quote must be in the note, or dropped ─> notify-by date

arvo/extract.py and arvo/rp.py make the two model calls; pricing.py, calendar_au.py and prices.py are the rules, fed by data/ndis_prices_2026_27.json, where every figure cites a document and page; voice.py hands audio to Gemma 4 directly; server.py plus one HTML file, on 127.0.0.1; eval/ holds every fixture, gold label and result, frozen under SHA-256 sums.
Gemma turns messy text into shifts and never picks a price, an item number or a deadline. For Nonna's Thursday evening its entire contribution is {"participant_id": "nonna", "date": "2026-11-05", "start": "19:00", "end": "21:30"}. The band, the item number and the $202.68 are code reading the Schedule. The model never saw a dollar sign.

The rule that matters most is s2.4(c) of the NDIS Pricing Schedule 2026-27 (p5): "Where a support a support crosses between different times of day or days of week and is delivered by a single worker, the higher of the amounts applies to the whole support." (The doubled words are in the official PDF.) In Arvo it is a test, not a prompt:

def test_crosses_8pm_whole_shift_at_evening_not_split(roster):
    ln, _ = only(roster, "priya", "2026-10-14", "15:00", "20:30")
    # 5.5 x 81.07 = 445.885 -> ROUND_HALF_UP 445.89 (float round() would give 445.88)
    assert (ln.item_number, ln.quantity, ln.unit_price, ln.total) == (SELF["weekday_evening"], 5.5, 81.07, 445.89)
    assert ln.rule.startswith("Crosses 8pm: whole shift at Weekday Evening rate")
    assert "s2.4(c)" in ln.rule

Flags get the same split. Gemma must return its evidence as a sentence copied from the note, and find_verbatim checks it is there; if not, the flag is dropped with a warning. A model that paraphrases is a model that can invent.
No real participant data anywhere. 24 template weeks come from eval/gen_fixtures.py, gold from the generator, never a model. 8 "wild" weeks were written by another AI agent imitating tired people (run-on prose, unpunctuated dictation, strike-throughs, "odo 45213 to 45231"); a second model labelled them blind and agreed on 58 of 58 shifts. 42 restrictive-practice notes came from another agent; a test fails if any 5-word run of one appears in the prompt. Voice memos are Piper TTS. Prompts and code were tuned on 8 dev weeks only; everything else ran once on code frozen at tag eval-freeze-1.




Held-out set
Arvo (Gemma 4 e4b reads, code prices)
Baselines




Test split: 16 template weeks, 119 shifts
93.3% shifts exact; 10/16 weeks right to the cent
code-only parser 91.6%, 9/16; Gemma pricing the week itself 0/16, line recall 49.5%


Wild diaries: 8 weeks, 58 shifts
75.9% exact; $121 mean error per week; 2/8 to the cent
code-only 39.7%, $1,207 per week, 0/8; Gemma alone $366 per week, 0/8


Restrictive-practice notes: 42 (22 restraints, 20 innocent with trap words)
detection F1 88.9% (precision 87.0%, recall 90.9%); 1/20 innocent flagged
keyword list F1 45.7%, 5/20 flagged; gemma4:e2b F1 41.4%


Rendered photos of a paper diary: 4 weeks
90.0% exact; 2/4 to the cent

gemma4:e2b 76.7%, 1/4


My own handwriting: 1 week, 7 shifts, one run
0/7 exact; dates 7/7, start 6/7, end 5/7, names 1/7, distances lost; all 7 misses flagged



Voice memos: 10, voice never used in development
6/10 every field right; participant, date, start 10/10; word error rate 12.0%
(memos I tuned on: 11/12)



The first row embarrassed me: a hand-written parser with no model nearly matches Gemma on the template weeks (91.6% against 93.3%) with lower dollar error ($132 a week against $195). The templates were too regular to prove anything. The wild row is where the model earns its keep, and the notes are where size matters: e2b reads shifts almost as well as e4b (89.1% against 93.3%) and misses 16 of 22 restraints. Size buys judgement, not transcription.
Arvo got 14 of 58 wild shifts wrong. Read one by one, 7 were my own code overwriting a value Gemma had right, and code invented 2 phantom shifts out of the worker's corrections (~~12~~ 16km read as a 12-16 shift; 10-2. actually 10-1 split in two). What it said, against what was true:
tom 9 30 till 1 30 (wild week 2, dictated). Gemma: 09:30-13:30, right. My parser took "9" and "1" as the hours and wrote 09:00-13:00 over it: start set to 09:00 from '9 30 till 1 30' (model said 09:30).
twenty two k (same week). Gemma: 22 km, right. Code found no "22" in the diary and zeroed it.
odo 61044 to 61058 (week 7). Gemma: 10 km. True: 14. Code zeroed that too.
pri 9:30 to 12:15pm Sundy (test week 18). Gemma: Sunday 31 January, right. Code did not know "Sundy", fell back to the heading 29/1 - Priya and moved the shift to Friday, which changes the rate.
"Gave Jake his usual night meds at 8 off the chart". Gemma: chemical restraint. True: innocent; "off the chart" means read off the medication chart.
"I left her out on the back verandah with the screen door latched for an hour". Gemma: environmental restraint. True: a restraint, but seclusion.
Same 42 notes, gemma4:e2b: 6 of 22 restraints found, 16 missed.
Held-out voice, end times spoken as "half 11", "half 4" and "half 5": heard right in the transcript, end time wrong on all three. A car-noise memo came out as "Massdenic Copper".

The guardrails exist because a model can invent a time or a km figure; tuned on 8 template weeks, they were overconfident. The fix is a principle: code overrules the model only when its own reading is unambiguous and the model's value is impossible; otherwise the model's value stands and the disagreement becomes a warning the worker sees.




Frozen (held out)
After the fix (not held out)




Test split, exact shifts
93.3%
95.0%


Test split, weeks right to the cent
10/16
11/16


Wild, exact shifts
75.9%
94.8%


Wild, weeks right to the cent
2/8
7/8


Wild, mean $ error per week
$121
$68


Voice memos with every field right
6/10
8/10



The right-hand column is not held out: I fixed the code while looking at those exact diaries, so the wild number is the one I trust least. Two things got worse, the cost of the rule (eval/results/postfix/).
The verbatim-quote check proves the sentence exists in the note, nothing more. It cannot tell that the screen door was seclusion, not environmental restraint, or that "off the chart" is no restraint at all. On the 42 held-out notes it dropped 0 flags: a floor against invention, not evidence of judgement. Pricing is the same: code prices to the cent, but only the shift it is given. Move Priya's Sunday to Friday and the arithmetic is perfect and the invoice is wrong. So the worker sees every shift Gemma read, with its span, before any invoice.
I went looking for the 2026-27 "Pricing Arrangements and Price Limits", the PAPL, where the time-band and travel rules have always lived. There is none: for 2026-27 the NDIA published a prices-only Pricing Schedule, and ndis.gov.au still lists the 2025-26 PAPL v1.1 as current guidance. So the boundary rule comes from the Schedule (s2.4(c), p5), the km rules from the 2025-26 PAPL, and the JSON records the document and page for each figure. If a plan manager disputes a line, the argument is about a page, not about what a model was thinking.
Limits. Victoria, non-remote, standard-intensity self-care and community-access items only; 42 notes is a small set. The 5-business-day duty belongs to registered providers; an unregistered sole trader must not use regulated restrictive practices at all, and no official source gives her a deadline, so Arvo labels the date as the registered provider's and gives her the Commission's contact details. It flags; it does not decide. Not legal or compliance advice.
Data and credits: NDIS Pricing Schedule 2026-27 and NDIS Commission material; Business Victoria public holidays; Gemma 4 via Ollama; Piper voices for the synthetic memos; Comic Neue for the synthetic diary photos.
Shift notes are health information, "sensitive information" under s 6 of the Privacy Act, and the OAIC recommends not entering personal information into publicly available generative AI tools. A worker who pastes "Gave PRN lorazepam 0.5mg" and a name into a hosted chatbot has a problem before she has an invoice. With open weights the model runs on her laptop, the server binds to 127.0.0.1, and nothing leaves. That is the product, not a feature of it.

Where a closed model would win: a frontier model would likely read "9 30 till 1 30" and "half 4" better than a 4B model, and might tell seclusion from environmental restraint. It would still need the same pricing code, because right-to-the-cent is a rules job, and it would send disability health notes to someone else's server. That is the trade; for this job I take the local side.
Open also means offline, where the memo gets recorded; $0 a week in tokens behind a $12 subscription; and a model swap that is one flag, which is how I learned e2b reads nearly as well and judges much worse.
I built Arvo with Claude Code as my coding agent. It wrote most of the code and the first draft of this post; I set the brief, directed the video, wrote and photographed the handwriting test, and edited the write-up. The decision log is in JOURNEY.md.
Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 4 (gemma4:e4b and gemma4:e2b, open weights) through Ollama on the worker's machine, for typed text, photos of a paper diary (vision) and voice memos (audio in, no separate speech model). The held-out eval above is the case for it, including where it loses.
Best Use of GitHub Copilot. The category text says "automate your project with GitHub Actions". ci.yml runs the tests on every push; gemma-smoke.yml installs Ollama on a CPU-only runner, pulls gemma4:e2b and runs the whole pipeline and a one-week eval with no GPU and no key: run 38347559687. I did not use the Copilot coding agent.

Spain's official gazette (BOE) as JSON: a free Apify Actor for daily alerts
articles.description:
If you build compliance dashboards, legal alerts or news tooling for Spain, sooner or later you need the new laws, decrees and orders as data. The Official State Gazette (BOE, Boletín Oficial del Estado) publishes open data, but turning a daily summary into a clean, filtered, deduplicated feed is plumbing you would rather not write twice.
NormaWatch is a free, MIT-licensed Apify Actor that does this plumbing. It reads the BOE daily summary and returns the new general provisions (Section I) as JSON, with official links. Think of it as a small "BOE API" you can schedule.
Each item is metadata plus links, never the full text:
{
  "id": "BOE-A-2026-99999",
  "date": "2026-10-16",
  "bulletin": "BOE",
  "section": "1",
  "department": "MINISTERIO DE EJEMPLO",
  "epigraph": "Procedimientos administrativos",
  "title": "Orden EJE/0000/2026, de 15 de octubre, por la que se regula un procedimiento de ejemplo.",
  "urlHtml": "https://www.boe.es/diario_boe/txt.php?id=BOE-A-2026-99999",
  "urlPdf": "https://www.boe.es/boe/dias/2026/10/16/pdfs/BOE-A-2026-99999.pdf",
  "urlXml": "https://www.boe.es/diario_boe/xml.php?id=BOE-A-2026-99999",
  "retrievedAt": "2026-10-16T09:30:00.000Z",
  "normType": "Orden",
  "source": "Fuente de los datos: Agencia Estatal Boletín Oficial del Estado",
  "sourceUrl": "https://www.boe.es"
}

(This sample is invented, to show the shape. The repo also has real examples.) In the Apify console the same data appears as a table, and you can export JSON or CSV or read it through the Apify API.
Date range: up to 367 dates in one run, so you can backfill a year. Leave it empty for today.
Filters: department, title keywords, and norm type. The norm type is derived by the Actor from the title, so treat it as a hint, not an official field.
onlyNew: remembers what it already delivered, per filter combination, so a daily scheduled run returns only new items.
Notices: an optional summary by e-mail, Telegram or Slack.
Regional gazettes (optional): BOJA (Andalusia, CC BY 4.0) and DOG (Galicia, CC BY-SA 4.0). The DOG feed only holds the latest issue, so it works for daily runs, not for history. The Junta de Andalucía and the Xunta de Galicia are not involved and do not endorse it.
Section III (optional, off by default): a restricted, filtered subset. Because that section contains titles that name people, a text filter reduces the risk but cannot remove it. Review the output before sharing it.
Open the Actor on the Apify Store.
Run it once with a date range for your initial backfill.
Create a daily schedule with onlyNew: true and your filters, for example:




{
  "departments": ["hacienda"],
  "keywords": ["modelo", "orden"],
  "onlyNew": true,
  "maxItems": 200
}

Point a webhook, a spreadsheet or your own dashboard at the dataset, or turn on the built-in notice.
It requests one day at a time with a pause between requests, retries with backoff, stops after repeated failures and identifies itself with a User-Agent. A year-long run took about 7 minutes in a local test (367 requests, no failures); on Apify it may vary.
It is not an official BOE or AEBOE service, and the output is not an official text. For legal effect, use the text published by the Agency.
Metadata and links only. No full text.
The BOE has its own free alert service, "Mi BOE". NormaWatch adds exact filters, memory of what was already delivered, and structured data.
It is free to use; you only pay for your own Apify platform usage (the free plan has a monthly credit; check Apify's pricing page).
The documentation is in Spanish, with a short English summary at the top of the README.
Apify Store: https://apify.com/saidcveltran/normawatch-boe

Source (MIT): https://github.com/saidcveltran/normawatch-boe



Issues and ideas are welcome on GitHub. By AIskaron.

How to Deploy SafeLine WAF with Traefik Safely: A Routing Checklist
articles.description:
Traefik and SafeLine can occupy different positions in a web traffic path, but a successful deployment depends on clearly defining which component owns each responsibility. The supplied SafeLine documentation describes SafeLine as a self-hosted web application firewall and an HTTP/HTTPS reverse proxy. It receives traffic for an original website, filters malicious requests, and forwards safe traffic to the application (SafeLine introduction, Protecting an application).
That model gives you a useful starting point for a Traefik design: make the request path explicit before changing production DNS. For example, document whether clients reach Traefik first and then SafeLine, or whether SafeLine is the public reverse proxy and Traefik is behind it. The supplied SafeLine guides explain how to configure a protected application through SafeLine’s Web Admin Console, including the application domain, listening port, SSL setting where applicable, and upstream address. They do not provide a Traefik-specific configuration or establish a native integration, so treat the Traefik portion as an architecture and verification exercise rather than copying an unverified recipe.
Begin with ownership of ports and TLS. Only one service should be the intended public listener for each address and port. Record where HTTPS is terminated, how the next hop is reached, and whether the next hop expects HTTP or HTTPS. Confirm that the hostname used by clients resolves to the server where the public protection layer is running. SafeLine’s application guide specifically instructs administrators to resolve the configured domain to the IP address of the SafeLine server after adding the application (application configuration guide).
Next, verify the SafeLine host before deployment. The official deployment guide lists Linux, x86_64 or arm64 instruction architecture, Docker 20.10.14 or later, Docker Compose 2.0.0 or later, and a minimum environment of one CPU core, 1 GB memory, and 5 GB disk. It also documents ARM-specific environment settings and notes that ARM installations require a Pro license, while the Personal Edition is unsupported on ARM (SafeLine deployment guide). Use those documented requirements as a preflight checklist rather than assuming that a Traefik host automatically satisfies them.
After SafeLine is installed, use its Web Admin Console to add the application. The documented flow is to open the Applications page, choose Add Application, enter the domain, listening port, optional SSL setting, and upstream, then point DNS at the SafeLine server. When Traefik is part of the path, test each hop separately: client to public listener, public listener to the next proxy, proxy to SafeLine, and SafeLine to the original application. Check status codes, redirects, host headers, request paths, and access logs at every boundary.
Keep a rollback plan based on DNS and listener ownership. Before switching traffic, record the original upstream, current certificates, ports, and health checks. Test an ordinary request first, then confirm that SafeLine records and blocks representative attack patterns. The official guide gives examples for SQL injection, XSS, path traversal, code injection, and XXE, and says attack details can be reviewed in the SafeLine Web Console (application testing guide). Perform security testing only against an application you control.
The supplied official documents explain SafeLine’s reverse-proxy model and application configuration, but they do not document a Traefik provider, middleware, labels, or a ready-made Traefik integration. A responsible deployment therefore starts by validating the network path and proxy responsibilities instead of assuming compatibility from similar proxy products.
There is no single placement established by the supplied sources. Choose the order that gives SafeLine a clear, reachable upstream and preserves the intended client request information. Then test the complete path, including TLS behavior, redirects, hostnames, and failure handling. Document the decision so future routing changes do not accidentally bypass the WAF.
Install SafeLine, sign in to the Web Admin Console, open Applications, and select Add Application. Enter the application domain, SafeLine listening port, SSL option when needed, and the real upstream address. Finally, resolve the domain to the SafeLine server as described in the official application guide.
Send normal application requests and inspect the result at each proxy boundary. Then use controlled test cases from the official guide, such as SQL injection, XSS, path traversal, code injection, or XXE, and check the SafeLine attack list and event details in the Web Console. Do not test systems without authorization.
Use this checklist to design your Traefik and SafeLine path, validate every hop, and document the final ownership of DNS, TLS, ports, and upstream routing. Review the SafeLine GitHub project and the official SafeLine documentation for the current project and deployment guidance.
SafeLine has surpassed 700,000 installations worldwide as of September 30, 2026. To celebrate, SafeLine Pro annual promotional pricing is $650-$880, compared with the regular $1,000 per year. See the offer details: https://cyberserval.tech/landing/lto

articles.title: China bloqueia 40 tecnologias de IA: o que isso muda na sua cadeia?
articles.description:
Restrições à exportação de IA na China: 40 tecnologias estratégicas que vão mudar sua cadeia de suprimentos (abril 2024)



  
  
  Introdução


A China acabou de apertar o cerco sobre 40 categorias de tecnologias críticas – de chips de 7 nm a bibliotecas de aprendizado de máquina – e a partir de abril de 2024 o novo regime de controle entra em vigor. O anúncio, feito pelos ministérios do Comércio (MOFCOM) e da Indústria e Tecnologia da Informação (MIIT), disparou buscas no Google Trends e deixou fabricantes, desenvolvedores e startups ocidentais em alerta máximo. Se sua empresa depende de componentes chineses para IA, data centers ou IoT, este artigo traz tudo que você precisa saber para se adequar rapidamente, incluindo um checklist de conformidade e um script Python pronto para monitorar as mudanças via APIs públicas.



Área
Exemplos de itens incluídos




Semicondutores
Chips avançados ≤ 7 nm, módulos DDR5, GPUs de treinamento IA


Equipamentos de fabricação
Máquinas de litografia EUV, sistemas de inspeção de wafer


Infraestrutura de computação
Servidores de alta performance, racks de data center


Software e frameworks
Bibliotecas de treinamento (TensorFlow, PyTorch), otimizadores de compilação, ferramentas de criptografia avançada


Sensores e IoT
Câmeras de alta resolução, módulos de comunicação 5G/6G


Outros
Sistemas de vigilância, kits de desenvolvimento de IA embarcada



Prepare a documentação – descrição detalhada do uso final, comprovação de que o produto não será destinado a fins militares ou de vigilância e plano de mitigação de risco.


Submeta o pedido – portal oficial do MOFCOM (https://exportlicense.mofcom.gov.cn).


Acompanhe o processo – o tempo médio varia entre 30 e 90 dias; esteja pronto para fornecer informações adicionais.




  
  
  Modelo de e‑mail de solicitação (exemplo)





Assunto: Pedido de Licença de Exportação – [Nome da Empresa] – [Código do Produto]

Prezados,

Segue anexo o formulário de solicitação (Formulário A) contendo:
1. Descrição completa do produto (modelo, número de série);
2. Destino final (país, cliente, uso previsto);
3. Declaração de não‑militarização;
4. Plano de mitigação de risco (controles de acesso, criptografia).

Aguardamos orientação sobre os próximos passos.

Atenciosamente,
[Nome] – [Cargo] – [Contato]

Multas: até 5 % do valor total da transação.


Bloqueio de exportações futuras: suspensão automática até a regularização.


Inclusão em lista negra internacional: proibição de operar com parceiros chineses por até 5 anos.
Crescimento explosivo da IA – Em 2023 o mercado global de IA ultrapassou US $150 bi; 70 % das infraestruturas de treinamento ainda dependem de chips fabricados na China (IC Insights).


Geopolítica em mudança – As tensões EUA‑China transformaram a tecnologia em questão de segurança nacional; a China busca preservar sua vantagem competitiva e impedir a transferência de know‑how.


Efeito cascata nas cadeias – A ASML já relata atrasos na entrega de máquinas de litografia; montadoras enfrentam escassez de DDR5, elevando o preço médio desses módulos em 30 % nos últimos três meses.



Item
Ação
Responsável
Prazo




Mapeamento de componentes
Inventariar todos os chips, softwares e sensores chineses usados nos produtos.
Engenharia de Suprimentos
1 semana


Classificação
Verificar cada item na lista dos 40 itens críticos.
Compliance
2 dias


Licença
Preparar e submeter pedidos de licença para os itens classificados.
Jurídico/Exportação
3 semanas


Monitoramento
Implementar alerta automático de mudanças na lista via API do MOFCOM.
TI
5 dias


Treinamento
Capacitar equipes de compras e desenvolvimento sobre as novas regras.
RH/Compliance
2 semanas


Revisão contratual
Atualizar cláusulas de fornecimento para incluir requisitos de licença.
Jurídico
1 semana



import requests, json, time

API_URL = "https://api.mofcom.gov.cn/export-restrictions/v1/items"
HEADERS = {"Accept": "application/json"}

def obter_itens():
    resp = requests.get(API_URL, headers=HEADERS)
    return resp.json() if resp.status_code == 200 else []

def comparar_lista(atual, anterior):
    novas = [i for i in atual if i not in anterior]
    removidas = [i for i in anterior if i not in atual]
    return novas, removidas

def main():
    lista_antiga = []
    while True:
        lista_atual = obter_itens()
        novas, removidas = comparar_lista(lista_atual, lista_antiga)
        if novas:
            print("Novos itens restritos:", novas)
        if removidas:
            print("Itens removidos da restrição:", removidas)
        lista_antiga = lista_atual
        time.sleep(86400)  # verifica a cada 24h

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Dica: agende o script em um container Docker e envie alertas para o Slack usando um webhook.
Diversificar fornecedores – buscar alternativas em Taiwan, Coreia do Sul e EUA para chips e módulos de memória.


Redesign de arquitetura – substituir componentes críticos por soluções baseadas em FPGA ou ASIC desenvolvidos internamente.


Licenças cruzadas – negociar acordos de transferência de tecnologia com parceiros que já possuam licenças válidas.


Estoque de segurança – manter buffer de 3‑6 meses para os itens mais sensíveis, evitando interrupções inesperadas.
As novas restrições chinesas não são apenas um obstáculo burocrático; elas remodelam a forma como a indústria global de IA se abastece e desenvolve. Quem agir rapidamente – mapeando componentes, solicitando licenças e implantando monitoramento automático – reduzirá custos de interrupção e ganhará vantagem competitiva. Use o checklist acima e o script Python como ponto de partida; a conformidade hoje é a base da inovação de amanhã.

articles.title: リアルタイムのマルウェア防御: AWS Network Firewall のアクティブ脅威防御の活用
articles.description: サイバー脅威は急速に進化しており、潜在的な問題を抱えるワークロードは 90 秒以内に脅威アクターに発見されます。この記事では、AWS Network Firewall のアクティブ脅威防御を紹介します。アクティブ脅威防御は、Amazon のハニーポットネットワーク MadPot の脅威インテリジェンスを活用し、30 分以内に保護ルールを自動でデプロイします。DNS、HTTP、TLS SNI、IP の各レイヤーでブロックするスイスチーズモデルの多層防御によって、攻撃キルチェーンの各段階を阻止します。また、Amazon GuardDuty との連携に加え、CVE-2025-48703 を悪用して Mythic C2 フレームワークをデプロイしようとした実際の攻撃を阻止した事例も解説します。

articles.title: Buddy AI: A Local AI Companion That Keeps Things Simple
articles.description:
Buddy AI: A Local AI Companion That Keeps Things Simple


This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady
Meet Buddy AI, a multimodal AI companion designed to make everyday interactions with AI simple, accessible, and more personal.
We often use AI to brainstorm ideas, ask questions, understand information, or get help with everyday tasks. But constantly switching between tools, writing detailed prompts, and relying on cloud-based services can make these simple activities more complicated than they need to be.
I built Buddy AI to explore a simpler approach: an AI companion powered by an open-weight Gemma model that users can interact with through a lightweight web interface.
The project uses Python and Flask for the backend, with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript powering the frontend. The goal is to keep the experience straightforward while exploring local AI inference and multimodal interaction.
The idea is simple: let AI handle some of the thinking and typing, so you can focus on what matters.
I built Buddy AI using a lightweight Python-based web application architecture.
The main components are:
Gemma: The open-weight AI model powering the companion's responses.
Python: Handles the application's backend logic.
Flask: Connects the backend to the web interface.
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: Provide the user interface and interaction layer.
One of my goals was to keep the application lightweight and avoid unnecessary complexity. I also focused on making the AI interaction efficient, including minimizing unnecessary token usage.
Rather than treating AI as an external feature bolted onto a conventional application, I wanted the model itself to be a core part of the experience.
Open innovation matters because AI should not be limited to applications that depend entirely on closed APIs.
Building Buddy AI around an open-weight model gave me the opportunity to experiment with the model-driven application architecture, explore local inference, and consider how developers can build AI experiences with greater control over their technology stack.
This approach offers several potential advantages:
Greater control: Developers can choose how and where to run a supported model.
Privacy opportunities: Local inference can help keep prompts and personal information on the user's machine, depending on the complete application architecture.
Flexibility: Open-weight models make it easier to experiment with different models and configurations.
Cost awareness: Local inference can reduce per-request API charges, although hardware and electricity still have costs.
Learning by building: Developers can explore how AI models integrate with real applications instead of treating them as black boxes.
For me, the most important part is the freedom to experiment, learn, and improve without making a closed API the foundation of every interaction.

articles.title: 27,288 vCenter and 413,891 ESXi Assets: A Virtualization Management Baseline
articles.description:
27,288 vCenter and 413,891 ESXi Assets: A Virtualization Management Baseline


The virtualization layer is where an organization's computing actually lives. It is also where the management interfaces are frequently forgotten, because they are deployed by the team that runs infrastructure rather than by the team that runs security tooling.
A measurement session on 20 October 2026 gives a working baseline for the exposure of that layer.
Queries ran between 22:33 and 22:37 UTC with sub_type="all" and a page size of one record.



Query
Matched assets




app="VMware ESXi"
413,891


app="VMware vCenter"
27,288


app="VMware vCenter" && country="US"
5,816


app="Kubernetes"
1


app="SonarQube"
12,022



The ratio between hypervisors and their management plane is roughly fifteen to one in observable data. That ratio is a useful planning input, and it also illustrates why the management count matters more than its size suggests.
An ESXi host is a hypervisor. Compromise of one host affects the virtual machines on that host.
A vCenter instance manages many hosts. Compromise of vCenter reaches every host it manages, and from there every virtual machine, plus the credentials used for backup, storage and network integration.
The fifteen-to-one ratio describes the leverage: one management compromise covers fifteen hosts on average. That is the concentration risk that makes vCenter a recurring target and why its management interface placement matters more than the hypervisor's.
The United States share of vCenter exposure — 5,816 of 27,288, about 21% — is lower than the WordPress concentration measured in the same session. That is consistent with vCenter being deployed on-premises in enterprise data centres rather than concentrated in a small number of cloud regions.
app="Kubernetes" returned 1. That result should not be read as evidence that one Kubernetes cluster exists on the internet.
Kubernetes is not a product with a single identifying response. It is a platform of components: an API server, an ingress controller, a dashboard, a kubelet on each node. A fingerprint labelled "Kubernetes" in a product database may correspond to a narrow detection pattern, or to almost nothing.
This is the same class of artefact discussed for other queries: a product name that does not map to a distinctive observable signature produces a count that describes the signature rather than the deployment. Container orchestration exposure requires querying the specific components — API servers, dashboards, and the various ingress implementations — not the platform name.
The contrast with SonarQube at 12,022 is instructive. A code quality platform has a distinct web interface with recognizable markers, so its fingerprint is meaningful. A platform assembled from separately deployed components is not.
For a virtualization estate, the practical sequence is:
Enumerate ESXi hosts and vCenter instances from the hypervisor management tooling — this is authoritative and requires no external data.
Determine which management interfaces answer from outside the administrative network, and whether any answer from the public internet.
Restrict those interfaces at the network layer, not only through application authentication.
Establish a patch baseline for the management plane separately from the hypervisor baseline, since the update mechanisms differ.
Prepare a credential inventory for vCenter's integrations: SSO, backup, storage, network.
Step five is frequently omitted and matters disproportionately. A vCenter compromise exposes integration credentials that grant access far beyond the virtualization layer, including to backup systems — which brings a recovery problem into an availability incident.
The 27,288 figure is useful for one specific conversation: an organization that believes it has no internet-reachable vCenter. If a scan finds a vCenter management interface on the organization's address space, that belief is wrong and correctable.
It is not useful for estimating exploitability. Whether a given vCenter is patched, whether SSO is enforced, whether the interface is behind a jump host — none of that is observable, and all of it determines the outcome.
