El nivel Tier0 permite 3 solicitudes por minuto, y cada turno de un bucle de herramientas es una solicitud. Una ejecución de agente de cinco turnos ya supera un minuto en ese nivel, así que presupuesta 10 $ acumulados antes de probar agentes en serio.
Una prueba de contrato detecta el día en que tu bucle de herramientas deja de recibir tool_calls. Deja que tu agente de programación la construya con Apidog CLI. Instala e inicia sesión una vez:
npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
apidog skill install

Luego indica a Claude Code, Codex o el agente que uses:
In Apidog project <projectId>, create an environment for https://api.moonshot.ai/v1
and an endpoint for POST /chat/completions. Add a test case that sends model
kimi-k3.1-pro, reasoning_effort "low", one get_order_status tool and
tool_choice "required". Assert status 200 and that choices[0].message.tool_calls
is non-empty. Run it and report failures.

El agente lee el esquema, valida su payload y ejecuta el caso:
apidog environment create kimi-prod --project <projectId> --base-url https://api.moonshot.ai/v1
apidog endpoint create --project <projectId> --file ./endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file case.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <envId> -r cli,json

Los casos de prueba necesitan una categoría válida; apidog test-case category --project <projectId> las lista. Una vez que la ejecución pase, cambia -r cli,json por -r junit con --out-dir y la misma comprobación controlará tu CI, como muestra nuestra guía de CI/CD con Apidog CLI. La configuración del agente está en Apidog CLI en Claude Code. El plan gratuito de Apidog cubre hasta 4 usuarios.
  
  



  
  
  Preguntas frecuentes



  
  
  ¿Cuál es la URL base de la API de Kimi K3.1 Pro?


https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 para Chat Completions y la API de Responses, y https://api.moonshot.ai/anthropic para la API de Messages compatible con Anthropic.
thinking?


No. El razonamiento siempre está activado. Contrólalo con el campo reasoning_effort de nivel superior ("low", "high" o "max").
Lee error.type. engine_overloaded_error es capacidad del servidor y una recarga no lo solucionará. rate_limit_reached_error significa los límites de tu nivel, y Tier0 solo permite 3 RPM.
Un campo de lectura de caché distinto de cero en usage significa un acierto: prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens en Chat Completions o cache_read_input_tokens en Messages.
No. La API requiere una recarga mínima de 1 $. El chat gratuito en la app de Kimi es la vía de 0 $, tratada en cómo usar Kimi K3.1 Pro gratis. Para conocer el modelo, consulta qué es Kimi K3.1 Pro.

articles.title: A beginner's guide to the Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Quantized model by Abenzerps on Huggingface
articles.description:
This is a simplified guide to an AI model called Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Quantized maintained by Abenzerps. If you like these kinds of analysis, you should join AImodels.fyi or follow us on Twitter.
Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Quantized is a set of quantized local image-generation weights based on the upstream Qwen-Image-2.1 model. Maintained by abenzerps, it provides GGUF, Safetensors, and Apple Silicon–oriented MLX files for use with ComfyUI. Its defining practical feature is the absence of a built-in safety checker or content filter: prompts can produce adult, NSFW, and sensitive imagery without refusals or blacked-out outputs. The README does not specify the model architecture beyond identifying it as an image-generation model, nor does it give a parameter count, training data, training steps, output resolution, or measured generation speed. Plan around the full component set, not just the diffusion file: ComfyUI also needs a Qwen3-VL 8B text encoder and a VAE. The repository reports 2,188,658 downloads, but that figure does not establish image quality or performance.
Local generation of adult or sensitive imagery. The release explicitly removes built-in safety filtering, so it suits workflows where a safety checker would block intended prompts. That also means the operator is responsible for prompt handling, access controls, and compliance with applicable laws and platform rules.
ComfyUI workflows with limited GPU memory. The GGUF options include a 4.60 GB Q4_K_M diffusion file, and the README recommends keeping the diffusion model in GPU VRAM while running or offloading the text encoder to system RAM. This separates the component that runs during sampling from text encoding, which runs once per prompt.
Apple Silicon image-generation setups. The repository includes MLX 4-bit, 6-bit, and 8-bit variants, described as optimized for Apple Silicon. These provide a platform-specific option rather than requiring a GGUF or GPU-oriented Safetensors file.
Local experimentation across quality and memory tradeoffs. The available formats range from 4.00 GB MLX 4-bit and 4.05 GB base Q4_0 GGUF to 14.23 GB BF16 GGUF. This lets practitioners compare quantization levels in their own workflow, though the README provides no measured quality or speed results for each variant.
Text-to-image and image-editing workflows in ComfyUI. The README points to official Comfy-Org templates for both tasks. It does not provide task-specific benchmark scores, so test the intended prompts and edit cases before relying on it in production.
The README does not report output resolution, parameter count, training data, training compute, inference speed, or benchmark methodology. The benchmark image is provided, but no numerical results or hardware details accompany it. Do not infer a resolution, quality level, or generation time from the file sizes.
The smallest diffusion files reduce storage and memory needs, but quantization can involve quality tradeoffs; the repository recommends Q4_K_M as a size-quality balance for GGUF without publishing comparative measurements. The full setup also has substantial memory and storage demands: the text encoder is 17.53 GB in BF16 or 9.35 GB in INT8, and the VAE is 676 MB. The recommended lower-memory arrangement places the INT8 text encoder in system RAM and the Q4_K_M diffusion model in VRAM. The README’s description of this as saving “9–17 GB” of VRAM is consistent with the listed encoder sizes; it does not give a minimum system RAM or GPU VRAM requirement.
The model has no built-in content filter. That is a deliberate property, not a guarantee that every prompt will produce a particular result. The README does not document other known image-quality failure modes, biases, or safety mitigations.
The stated license is the Qwen Research License, described in the repository as “other.” The provided information does not establish commercial-use rights or the license terms, so review the license before commercial deployment.
Qwen-Image-2.1-GGUF is the better fit if you want the same upstream Qwen-Image-2.1 base weights in GGUF without choosing this release’s explicitly uncensored package. This model is the clearer choice when the absence of a built-in safety checker is a requirement and when you want additional formats such as Safetensors and MLX; the supplied information does not provide measured speed or quality differences between them. The alternative’s notice says a fully uncensored version is in development, so check its current status before choosing it for an uncensored workflow.
Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Abenzerps-GGUF is another GGUF distribution of uncensored Qwen-Image-2.1 weights. Choose this model if you need the documented Safetensors or MLX variants, companion text encoder and VAE files, and ComfyUI setup guidance in one repository; choose the alternative if its distribution better matches your existing GGUF workflow. The provided information does not establish a quality, speed, or cost advantage for either distribution.
Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-GGUF is another uncensored GGUF option based on the same upstream model. This repository is a stronger fit when you want multiple non-GGUF quantization formats and explicit companion-file instructions. The alternative’s notice reports a Q8_0 tensor shape mismatch in ComfyUI during sampling and recommends Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, or Q6_K instead; the supplied information does not confirm whether that issue applies to this model’s Q8_0 file.
Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-GGUF is also described as an uncensored GGUF distribution using the upstream base weights. Pick this model for the documented MLX and Safetensors choices, or the alternative if its repository and files suit your existing setup. No comparative benchmark, inference-speed, or cost data is provided, so there is no supported basis to claim that one produces better images or runs faster.
Qwen-Image-2.1-GGUF targets low-VRAM ComfyUI use with GGUF quantizations and describes its quantization as reducing memory pressure while preserving detail, composition, and prompt alignment. This model is the better fit when you need an explicitly uncensored release and Apple Silicon MLX or Safetensors options; the alternative may suit a workflow centered on its stated low-VRAM GGUF profile. The supplied information does not provide comparable hardware tests or measured quality results.
Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Quantized packages quantized versions of the upstream Qwen-Image-2.1 weights. The source revision is b3179ad355be050328e483a9dfdd9e60cd62adfa. The README identifies conversion using stable-diffusion.cpp commit 1330cebae8f2ba99249df846cc0c9444fcbd4308 and comfy-kitchen. The text encoder and VAE source is Comfy-Org/Qwen-Image-2.1. The stated license is the Qwen Research License.
Available uncensored diffusion files:



Format or quantization
File size




BF16 GGUF
14.23 GB


FP8 Safetensors
6.63 GB


INT8 ConvRot Safetensors
6.76 GB


NVFP4 Safetensors
4.20 GB


MLX 4-bit Safetensors
4.00 GB


MLX 6-bit Safetensors
5.78 GB


MLX 8-bit Safetensors
7.56 GB


Q8_0 GGUF
7.59 GB


Q6_K GGUF
5.88 GB


Q5_K_M GGUF
5.22 GB


Q4_K_M GGUF
4.60 GB


Q4_0 GGUF
4.15 GB



The repository also lists non-UC GGUF files: Q8_0 at 7.59 GB, Q6_K at 5.88 GB, Q5_K_M at 5.22 GB, Q4_K_M at 4.60 GB, and Q4_0 at 4.05 GB. It recommends Q4_K_M for the best balance of GGUF size and quality. It describes INT8 ConvRot and NVFP4 as high-performance options on supported GPUs, without naming supported GPU models or providing speed measurements. MLX files target Apple Silicon.
ComfyUI companion files are a Qwen3-VL 8B text encoder in BF16 (17.53 GB) or INT8 ConvRot (9.35 GB), plus a BF16 VAE (676 MB). The README recommends the INT8 encoder for lower memory use. It suggests keeping the diffusion model in GPU VRAM and running or offloading the text encoder to system RAM; text encoding runs once per prompt. For VRAM out-of-memory errors, it recommends starting ComfyUI with --lowvram.
Supported workflow components include ComfyUI, the leejet/ComfyUI-GGUF custom node, ComfyUI’s UNETLoader, CLIPLoader, and VAELoader nodes, and official Comfy-Org text-to-image and image-edit workflow templates. For GGUF, use Unet Loader (GGUF); for Safetensors, use UNETLoader. Set the text encoder’s CLIPLoader type to qwen_image. The README warns that the older city96/ComfyUI-GGUF may produce an “Unknown model architecture!” error; it recommends the leejet fork or adding ModelQwenImage to tools/convert.py.
The README does not specify architecture details beyond the image-generation task, parameter count, training dataset, training steps, compute, maximum resolution, inference speed, or batch-size guidance.
Text prompts: The model is presented for text-to-image generation. The README does not specify prompt syntax, token limits, or supported languages.
Image inputs: An official image-edit workflow template is listed, but the README does not document accepted image formats, dimensions, or editing constraints.
Runtime components: A diffusion-model file, a Qwen3-VL 8B text encoder, and a VAE are required for the documented ComfyUI setup. Choose a compatible diffusion quantization and encoder precision.
Generated images: The repository describes local image generation and provides text-to-image and image-edit workflow templates. It does not specify output resolution, image format, or post-processing requirements.
Content filtering: The release has no built-in safety checker or content filter; output behavior depends on prompts and the execution environment.
The README documents a ComfyUI workflow rather than a Python inference API, so it does not provide a supported Python model-loading or generation call. To run the documented setup, place the selected diffusion file in ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models/, the text encoder in ComfyUI/models/text_encoders/, and the VAE in ComfyUI/models/vae/. For example, use qwen-image-2.1-UC-Q4_K_M.gguf, qwen3vl_8b_int8_convrot.safetensors, and qwen_image_2.1_vae_bf16.safetensors.
Install the maintained ComfyUI-GGUF fork in ComfyUI/custom_nodes/:
cd ComfyUI/custom_nodes
git clone https://github.com/leejet/ComfyUI-GGUF

In ComfyUI, load the GGUF diffusion file with Unet Loader (GGUF). Load the text encoder with CLIPLoader and set its type to qwen_image; load the VAE with VAELoader. For a Safetensors diffusion file, use UNETLoader instead. If VRAM runs out, start ComfyUI with --lowvram. The README also points to official text-to-image and image-edit workflow templates.
Q: Can I use Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Quantized commercially?
A: The repository states the Qwen Research License. The provided information does not specify commercial-use permissions, so review the license terms before commercial use.
Q: How much VRAM do I need to run it?
A: No minimum VRAM requirement is stated. The recommended setup uses a Q4_K_M diffusion file of about 4.6 GB in VRAM and an INT8 text encoder of about 9.35 GB in system RAM; the VAE is 676 MB. Use --lowvram if ComfyUI reports a VRAM out-of-memory error.
Q: Which quantization should I choose for ComfyUI?
A: The README recommends Q4_K_M as the best balance of GGUF size and quality. It lists Q4_K_M at 4.60 GB, Q5_K_M at 5.22 GB, Q6_K at 5.88 GB, and Q8_0 at 7.59 GB, but does not publish comparative quality or speed measurements.
Q: How does it compare with Qwen-Image-2.1-GGUF for uncensored generation?
A: This release explicitly has no built-in safety checker or content filter. The similar model’s notice says a fully uncensored version is in development, so this release is the documented choice when uncensored behavior is required now; the supplied information does not establish a quality or speed difference.
Q: What are the known image-quality issues?
A: The README provides a benchmark image but no numerical results, documented failure modes, or output-resolution details. It recommends Q4_K_M for a GGUF size-quality balance, but does not quantify quality loss across quantizations.
Q: Can I fine-tune this model?
A: The README documents quantized files for local inference through ComfyUI, not a fine-tuning workflow. It does not specify fine-tuning support or a training framework.
Q: How fast is inference, and what batch size should I use?
A: The README gives no inference-time, throughput, or batch-size measurements. It says to keep the diffusion model in GPU VRAM because speed matters during sampling, and to run or offload the text encoder to system RAM because it encodes once per prompt.
Q: Does the model filter NSFW prompts?
A: No. The release has no built-in safety checker or content filter and can generate adult, NSFW, and sensitive imagery without prompt refusals or blacked-out images.

articles.title: Taming SQLAlchemy Implicit Flushes: Mitigating Unexpected Deadlocks and Serialization Failures Under High Concurrency
articles.description:
Taming SQLAlchemy Implicit Flushes: Mitigating Unexpected Deadlocks and Serialization Failures Under High Concurrency


Database deadlocks in high-throughput applications are rarely the result of overt logic errors. In many Python services built on SQLAlchemy, they stem from an ergonomic feature operating silently in the background: implicit autoflush. 
When building high-concurrency microservices, developers often focus on choosing between optimistic locking (version checking) and pessimistic locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE). However, if your ORM flushes state to the database at unpredictable junctures, your locking sequence will invert, holding exclusive row locks far longer than anticipated and triggering deadlocks (OperationalError: DeadlockDetected or database-specific errors like PostgreSQL's 40P01 / MySQL's 1213).
This article analyzes how SQLAlchemy’s implicit autoflush triggers concurrency collisions, details an architectural pattern incorporating explicit flush boundaries, Pydantic v2 data validation, and jittered exponential backoff, and provides a deep dive into environment diagnostics and production infrastructure readiness.
By default, SQLAlchemy initializes its Session with autoflush=True. Under this setting, whenever a read query—such as session.execute(select(...)) or session.scalars(...)—is evaluated, SQLAlchemy inspects the session’s internal Identity Map for dirty or pending objects. If modified state exists in memory, SQLAlchemy silently executes an intermediate session.flush() before dispatching the SELECT query.
flowchart TD
    subgraph ClientSession ["Client Application Session"]
        A["Step 1: Mutate Model A in Memory"]
        B["Step 2: Run SELECT query for Model B"]
        C["Step 3: Mutate Model B"]
        D["Step 4: Explicit Commit"]
    end

    subgraph DatabaseEngine ["RDBMS (PostgreSQL / MySQL)"]
        E["Row A: Locked via Implicit Flush (UPDATE)"]
        F["Read Query Executed"]
        G["Row B: Locked (UPDATE)"]
        H["Transaction Completed (RELEASE ALL LOCKS)"]
    end

    A -- "Object marked dirty" --> B
    B -. "Implicit Autoflush triggered before SELECT" .-> E
    E -- "Proceed with read" --> F
    F --> C
    C --> D
    D -- "Flush remaining & COMMIT" --> G
    G --> H
This implicit behavior introduces three severe concurrency pitfalls:
Premature Row Lock Acquisition: Exclusive row-level locks (UPDATE / INSERT) are claimed earlier in the transaction lifecycle than expected, holding locks during subsequent computation or querying phases.
Lock Order Inversion: When two concurrent threads (Worker 1 and Worker 2) process overlapping entities, an uncoordinated implicit flush will alter the physical SQL execution order, resulting in circular wait conditions (deadlock).
Traceback Obfuscation: The resulting OperationalError does not fail at session.commit(), but rather at an innocuous session.scalars(select(...)) query, baffling engineers during incident triage.
To eliminate non-deterministic locking and build a resilient persistence layer, we adopt three design constraints:
Explicit Flush Control (autoflush=False): Disable automatic flushes at the session maker level. State transitions must cross the persistence boundary strictly when explicitly designated via session.flush() or session.commit().
Strict Domain Validation via Pydantic v2: Enforce model invariants, version checks, and serialization boundaries prior to modifying ORM entities in memory.
Resilient Retry Loop with Truncated Exponential Backoff & Full Jitter: Intercept database-level transient contention (OperationalError) and retry the entire transaction boundary with decorrelated delay patterns.
Below is the complete, self-contained verification script implementing these architectural requirements. It defines domain schemas with Pydantic v2 (featuring automated serialization fallback for high-performance orjson), explicit SQLAlchemy ORM models, transaction boundary managers, and a decorated retry mechanism with jittered backoff.
import time
import random
import logging
from typing import Generator, Dict, Any
from contextlib import contextmanager

try:
    import orjson
    HAS_ORJSON = True
except ImportError:
    import json
    HAS_ORJSON = False

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, Column, Integer, String, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base, sessionmaker, Session
from sqlalchemy.exc import OperationalError

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class AccountPayload(BaseModel):
    account_id: int = Field(..., gt=0)
    balance: int = Field(..., ge=0)
    version: int = Field(..., ge=0)

    def serialize(self) -> bytes:
        data_dict = self.model_dump()
        if HAS_ORJSON:
            return orjson.dumps(data_dict)
        else:
            return json.dumps(data_dict).encode("utf-8")

    @classmethod
    def deserialize(cls, data: bytes) -> "AccountPayload":
        if HAS_ORJSON:
            parsed = orjson.loads(data)
        else:
            parsed = json.loads(data.decode("utf-8"))
        return cls.model_validate(parsed)

    @classmethod
    def decode_to_dict(cls, data: bytes) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        if HAS_ORJSON:
            return orjson.loads(data)
        else:
            return json.loads(data.decode("utf-8"))

Base = declarative_base()

class AccountModel(Base):
    __tablename__ = "accounts"

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True, index=True)
    balance = Column(Integer, nullable=False, default=0)
    version = Column(Integer, nullable=False, default=0)

DATABASE_URL = "sqlite:///:memory:"
engine = create_engine(DATABASE_URL, echo=False, future=True)

# Session configured with autoflush=False to prevent mid-transaction implicit locks
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(
    bind=engine,
    class_=Session,
    autoflush=False,
    autocommit=False,
    expire_on_commit=False
)

def init_db():
    Base.metadata.create_all(bind=engine)
    with SessionLocal() as session:
        acc1 = AccountModel(id=1, balance=1000, version=0)
        acc2 = AccountModel(id=2, balance=1000, version=0)
        session.add_all([acc1, acc2])
        session.commit()

@contextmanager
def get_session() -> Generator[Session, None, None]:
    session = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield session
        session.commit()
    except Exception:
        session.rollback()
        raise
    finally:
        session.close()

def update_account_with_retry(account_id: int, amount: int, max_retries: int = 3) -> None:
    attempt = 0
    while attempt < max_retries:
        attempt += 1
        try:
            with get_session() as session:
                stmt = select(AccountModel).filter_by(id=account_id)
                account = session.scalars(stmt).first()

                if not account:
                    raise ValueError(f"Account {account_id} not found")

                payload = AccountPayload(
                    account_id=account.id,
                    balance=account.balance,
                    version=account.version
                )

                new_balance = payload.balance + amount
                if new_balance < 0:
                    raise ValueError("Insufficient funds")

                account.balance = new_balance
                account.version += 1

                # Explicitly flush changes to the DB when the domain state is complete
                session.flush()
                logger.info(f"Successfully updated Account {account_id}: new balance = {new_balance}")
                return

        except OperationalError as e:
            logger.warning(
                f"Lock conflict/deadlock detected on attempt {attempt}/{max_retries} for account {account_id}: {e}"
            )
            if attempt >= max_retries:
                logger.error(f"Max retries reached for account {account_id}. Aborting.")
                raise
            # Exponential Backoff with Jitter
            sleep_time = (2 ** attempt) + (random.randint(0, 1000) / 1000.0)
            time.sleep(sleep_time)

def run_verification():
    init_db()
    logger.info("Database initialized with test data.")

    update_account_with_retry(account_id=1, amount=500)
    update_account_with_retry(account_id=2, amount=-200)

    with SessionLocal() as session:
        acc1 = session.get(AccountModel, 1)
        acc2 = session.get(AccountModel, 2)

        p1 = AccountPayload(account_id=acc1.id, balance=acc1.balance, version=acc1.version)
        p2 = AccountPayload(account_id=acc2.id, balance=acc2.balance, version=acc2.version)

        logger.info(f"Final State Account 1: {AccountPayload.decode_to_dict(p1.serialize())}")
        logger.info(f"Final State Account 2: {AccountPayload.decode_to_dict(p2.serialize())}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_verification()

When executing verification scripts in fresh staging containers or CI environments, operations may fail immediately during bootstrap with an unhandled exception:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/phenox/gemini-sandbox/TOAI_Workspace/V2_SandBox/V2_PROD_20261025_051946_test.py", line 16, in <module>
    from sqlalchemy import create_engine, Column, Integer, String, select
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sqlalchemy'

This failure is not a flaw in transaction semantics, ORM mapping, or deadlock resolution logic. It represents an environment provision failure: the runtime environment lacks the required distribution package (sqlalchemy). 
Notice how the script gracefully handles performance optimizations:
try:
    import orjson
    HAS_ORJSON = True
except ImportError:
    import json
    HAS_ORJSON = False

While application-level conditional imports (e.g., falling back from orjson to Python standard library json) protect optional accelerators, foundational dependencies such as SQLAlchemy and Pydantic cannot be treated as optional. When the base interpreter environment lacks these dependencies, execution halts during AST evaluation before a single line of business logic can run.
Preventing execution drift between development, CI, and production requires treating environment provisioning with the same rigor applied to SQL isolation levels.
requirements.txt)


Declare core dependencies with explicit minimum version constraints to guarantee SQLAlchemy 2.0+ query syntax (select(), session.scalars()) and Pydantic v2 compatibility:
sqlalchemy>=2.0.0
pydantic>=2.0.0
orjson>=3.0.0

For deterministic production deployments, utilize lockfiles pinned to exact hashes via tools like pip-tools, uv, or poetry:
# Generating locked requirements with hashes
uv pip compile requirements.in --generate-hashes -o requirements.txt

In continuous integration pipelines and test runners, dependency synchronization must precede script evaluation:
# Upgrade build tools and install pinned dependencies
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements.txt

In containerized architectures (Docker/Kubernetes), bake dependencies directly into the immutable base image:
FROM python:3.11-slim

WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .
CMD ["python", "verification_script.py"]




Concern
Anti-Pattern
Recommended Solution




Session Flush Policy
Default autoflush=True triggering random intermediate flushes
Configure sessionmaker(..., autoflush=False) or isolate read blocks with session.no_autoflush



Lock Duration
In-memory mutations held while subsequent queries run
Defer mutations until required, execute explicitly via session.flush() directly before commit


Transient Contention
Raw failures on OperationalError deadlocks
Truncated exponential backoff with full jitter wrapped around the transaction boundary


Data Boundaries
Passing active ORM entities across external API boundaries
Validate and serialize via Pydantic v2 schemas (BaseModel) before and after persistence


Dependency Integrity
Ad-hoc package installations resulting in ModuleNotFoundError

Declarative dependency manifests (requirements.txt) enforced by automated containerized CI pipelines



Sophisticated transactional designs and concurrency controls cannot function without reproducible runtime environments. Ensuring strict synchronization between infrastructural manifests and transactional logic is essential for resilient, high-concurrency Python architectures.

articles.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro API: Endpoints, Tool Calling, Caching and Errors
articles.description:
The Kimi K3.1 Pro API runs at https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 with model IDs kimi-k3.1-pro and kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed. It speaks three wire formats: OpenAI Chat Completions, the Responses API and Anthropic Messages, so the SDKs you already use work with a changed base URL. The model unlocks after a $1 minimum top-up.
Try Apidog today


This is the reference for production code. For your first call, streaming and the Codex or Claude Code setups, read how to use Kimi K3.1 Pro; for costs, see Kimi K3.1 Pro pricing. Facts come from Moonshot's K3.1 Pro quickstart and linked docs, read October 24, 2026.
Moonshot exposes K3.1 Pro through three API surfaces. Pick the one your client library or agent already speaks; the model, key and billing are the same on all three.



Surface
Format
Endpoint
Typical client




Chat Completions
OpenAI
https://api.moonshot.ai/v1/chat/completions

openai SDK, most frameworks


Responses API
OpenAI Responses
https://api.moonshot.ai/v1/responses
Codex (wire_api = "responses")


Messages API
Anthropic
https://api.moonshot.ai/anthropic/v1/messages
Anthropic SDK, Claude Code



They differ in how you set the cache TTL and where usage lands (see caching below). Coming from K3? Our Kimi K3 API guide still applies; K3.1 Pro is a post-trained K3 with the same 1,048,576-token context.
You need a funded account and a key from the right product. Four steps:
Top up at least $1 on the Kimi API platform. K3.1 Pro is a flagship model and unlocks only after a successful top-up.
Create a key in the API keys console and export it as MOONSHOT_API_KEY.
Confirm the model is visible to that key with GET /v1/models.
Call kimi-k3.1-pro from code.




curl https://api.moonshot.ai/v1/models \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $MOONSHOT_API_KEY" | grep -o '"kimi-k3.1-pro[^"]*"'

If the model isn't listed, fix that first. Kimi API, Kimi Code and Kimi Membership are separate products: a Kimi Code key won't work on the API endpoint, and a membership doesn't become API balance.
Most OpenAI parameters behave as you'd expect. These are the ones that differ or catch people out:



Parameter
What to know




reasoning_effort
Top-level field: "low", "high" or "max" (default "max"). Thinking is always on.


thinking
Don't send it. K3.1 Pro doesn't support it; use reasoning_effort instead.


max_completion_tokens
Defaults to 131072. Maximum output is 1,048,576 minus your prompt tokens.


response_format

json_schema with strict: true. Parse message.content only, never reasoning_content.


partial
Put "partial": true on a final assistant message to continue from a prefix.


tool_choice

"required" forces at least one tool call; "auto" lets the model decide.


prompt_cache_options

{"mode": "implicit", "ttl": "5m" or "1h"} on Chat Completions and Responses.



Reasoning tokens count toward your usage, so use "low" for classification and extraction. Preserved Thinking is always on, so every assistant message goes back with its reasoning_content intact (thinking models guide).
A production tool loop on K3.1 Pro follows four rules from Moonshot's docs:
Force a tool call on the first turn with tool_choice="required", then switch to "auto".
Append the complete assistant message, reasoning_content and tool_calls included.
Send one tool message per tool_call_id.
Cap the number of turns so a confused model can't loop forever.




import json, os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI([REDACTED CREDENTIAL],
                base_url="https://api.moonshot.ai/v1")

TOOLS = [{"type": "function", "function": {
    "name": "get_order_status",
    "description": "Look up an order's shipping status by ID",
    "parameters": {"type": "object",
                   "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}},
                   "required": ["order_id"]}}}]

def get_order_status(order_id):
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is order A-1042?"}]
tool_choice = "required"
for _ in range(8):  # hard cap on turns
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="kimi-k3.1-pro", reasoning_effort="high",
        messages=messages, tools=TOOLS, tool_choice=tool_choice)
    msg = resp.choices[0].message
    messages.append(msg)  # whole message, not msg.content
    if not msg.tool_calls:
        print(msg.content)
        break
    for call in msg.tool_calls:
        result = get_order_status(**json.loads(call.function.arguments))
        messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id,
                         "content": json.dumps(result)})
    tool_choice = "auto"

The classic bug is appending msg.content instead of msg, which drops tool_calls and reasoning_content.
When your agent has dozens or hundreds of tools, don't send every definition on every request. Moonshot's K3 tool calling best practice recommends this flow:
Declare one search_tools function (your backend implements it) plus a few core tools.
Set tool_choice: "required" on the first turn so the model retrieves before answering.
Inject the matching tool definitions through a system message that carries a tools field.
Let the model call the loaded tools on later turns, with tool_choice back on "auto".




# after search_tools returns ["create_github_pr"]
messages.append({"role": "system",
                 "tools": [CATALOG["create_github_pr"]]})

Injected definitions use the top-level tools format and apply from that message onward. The server doesn't retain them, so keep the message in later requests. Neither changing tool_choice nor appending a definition breaks the prefix cache.
K3.1 Pro accepts images and video alongside text and returns text. Make content an array of parts: an image_url part (the quickstart example sends a base64 data URL, and notes public image URLs aren't supported) or a video_url part that points at an uploaded file with an ms:// ID.
from pathlib import Path

video = client.files.create(file=Path("demo.mp4"), purpose="video")
content = [{"type": "video_url", "video_url": {"url": f"ms://{video.id}"}},
           {"type": "text", "text": "Summarize this video."}]

Pass content as the user message, and delete the file with client.files.delete(video.id) when you're done.
Caching is automatic for repeated prefixes with a 5-minute default TTL. Cache hits bill at $0.20 per million tokens against $2.00 for uncached input, and a 1-hour write costs $4.00 against $2.00 for 5 minutes. On a 1M-token prefix, the 1-hour TTL pays for itself after two hits.
Put stable content first (system prompt, tool definitions, docs), changing content last, and no timestamps in the prefix. With the openai SDK, pass the TTL through extra_body:
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="kimi-k3.1-pro",
    messages=[{"role": "system", "content": DOCS},
              {"role": "user", "content": question}],
    extra_body={"prompt_cache_options": {"mode": "implicit", "ttl": "1h"}},
)
d = resp.usage.prompt_tokens_details
print(resp.usage.prompt_tokens, d.cached_tokens,
      getattr(d, "cache_write_tokens", 0))

The Anthropic API sets the TTL with a top-level cache_control field; markers inside messages are ignored:
curl https://api.moonshot.ai/anthropic/v1/messages \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $MOONSHOT_API_KEY" \
  --data '{"model": "kimi-k3.1-pro", "max_tokens": 256,
    "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"},
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]}'

Where cache usage shows up depends on the surface:



Surface
Cache read
Cache write




Chat Completions
usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens
usage.prompt_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens


Responses
usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens
usage.input_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens


Messages
usage.cache_read_input_tokens
usage.cache_creation_input_tokens



When streaming Chat Completions, set stream_options.include_usage=true to get usage in the final chunk. Each hit renews the TTL, which is locked at first write. Full rules: the context caching guide.
Most failures fall into six patterns. Check error.type on every 429, because the fix depends on it.



Symptom
Cause
Fix




401 or 404
Wrong product key, region mismatch, no balance, or wrong model name
Use a Kimi API key, check balance, confirm the model in GET /v1/models, clear stale env vars and proxies


429 engine_overloaded_error

Server capacity
Wait per Retry-After, back off, lower concurrency. Topping up won't help.


429 rate_limit_reached_error

Your org hit concurrency, RPM, TPM or TPD
Slow down or move up a tier


429 exceeded_current_quota_error

Low balance, overdue account or expired voucher
Check the balance API and top up


finish_reason: "length"
Output hit max_completion_tokens

Raise the limit or continue with partial mode


Same tool called again and again
Broken message layout
Append the message as-is, match every tool_call_id, assemble streamed tool_calls fully, then add client-side repeat detection



Watch retries. The OpenAI SDK retries 2 times by default on connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and 5xx, so one call can become three requests against your RPM. On a low tier, lower the client's max_retries and back off on error.type yourself. Requests interrupted by a 429 aren't charged.
If a third-party agent fails, call the API directly with the same key, endpoint and model. If that works, the tool is the problem. See the troubleshooting page and error codes.
Your cumulative top-up sets your tier on the limits page:



Tier
Cumulative top-up
Concurrency
RPM
TPM




Tier0
$1
1
3
500,000 (1.5M per day)


Tier1
$10
15
100
2,000,000


Tier2
$20
40
100
3,000,000


Tier3
$100
50
200
3,000,000


Tier4
$1,000
60
200
4,000,000


Tier5
$3,000
100
300
5,000,000



Tier0 allows 3 requests per minute, and every turn of a tool loop is a request. A five-turn agent run already spills past one minute at that tier, so budget $10 cumulative before you test agents seriously.
A contract test catches the day your tool loop stops getting tool_calls back. Let your coding agent build it with Apidog CLI. Install and log in once:
npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
apidog skill install

Then prompt Claude Code, Codex or whichever agent you use:
In Apidog project <projectId>, create an environment for https://api.moonshot.ai/v1
and an endpoint for POST /chat/completions. Add a test case that sends model
kimi-k3.1-pro, reasoning_effort "low", one get_order_status tool and
tool_choice "required". Assert status 200 and that choices[0].message.tool_calls
is non-empty. Run it and report failures.

The agent reads the schema, validates its payload and runs the case:
apidog environment create kimi-prod --project <projectId> --base-url https://api.moonshot.ai/v1
apidog endpoint create --project <projectId> --file ./endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file case.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <envId> -r cli,json

Test cases need a valid category; apidog test-case category --project <projectId> lists them. Once the run passes, swap -r cli,json for -r junit with --out-dir and the same check gates your CI, as our Apidog CLI CI/CD guide shows. Agent setup lives in Apidog CLI in Claude Code. Apidog's Free plan covers up to 4 users.
  
  



  
  
  FAQ



  
  
  What is the base URL for the Kimi K3.1 Pro API?


https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 for Chat Completions and the Responses API, and https://api.moonshot.ai/anthropic for the Anthropic-compatible Messages API.
thinking parameter?


No. Thinking is always on. Control it with the top-level reasoning_effort field ("low", "high" or "max").
Read error.type. engine_overloaded_error is server capacity and a top-up won't fix it. rate_limit_reached_error means your tier's limits, and Tier0 allows only 3 RPM.
A non-zero cache read field in usage means a hit: prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens on Chat Completions or cache_read_input_tokens on Messages.

articles.title: Backend Task Monitoring Tools — Node.js Watchdogs vs Health Check APIs, Choose by Evidence
Egress allowlists need destination identity and a bounded IP range
articles.description:
Egress allowlists need destination identity and a bounded IP range


An internal service can make outbound requests to package registries, model providers, webhooks, and partner APIs. Those connections are often treated as normal infrastructure traffic. If the service is compromised, the same network path can become a channel for data exfiltration, command-and-control, or access to a cloud metadata endpoint. An egress allowlist narrows that path, but only when it identifies the destination and protocol that the application actually needs.
An allowlist based on a broad IP range is easy to bypass when the destination uses a content delivery network or a shared cloud address. A hostname rule can also be too broad if it permits every path and method on a shared domain. The policy should combine a destination, a port, a protocol, and, where the proxy understands it, a path or TLS server name. The goal is to make the permitted traffic attributable to a use case.
List each outbound dependency and the exact service, region, port, and protocol it requires. Record whether the connection is a public API, a private endpoint, a package mirror, or a webhook. Put the owner and expiry on every exception. A wildcard entry should be a reviewed temporary control, not the default that makes an application work.
For HTTP traffic, enforce policy at an egress proxy or gateway where it can inspect the destination host, TLS server name, and request method. A layer 3 network policy can permit or deny addresses, but it may not know that a broad service address belongs to an unrelated tenant. Pair network policy with application-level authorization and a trusted DNS resolver.
When a Kubernetes workload needs an external service, an implementation may expose an explicit service entry or gateway route. Istio's egress guidance describes changing from an allow-any mode to a registry-only mode and creating a service entry for each approved destination. Gateway API documentation warns that external hostname backends still depend on DNS trust and recommends egress domain allowlists plus admission and network controls. Those controls address different failure modes.
Cloud metadata endpoints are not ordinary external dependencies. Block application access to metadata addresses unless the workload has a documented identity-federation need. Use a managed identity path that limits token scope, and test from the workload rather than assuming a network policy covers the host's routing table.
DNS is part of the policy. A hostname allowlist that follows a DNS answer chosen by an untrusted resolver can be redirected. Use a controlled resolver, resolve internally, and apply policy to the resolved destination and the original host or TLS identity where possible. Protect the configuration that changes DNS records and monitor for new names that resolve to the same destination ranges.
Logging must show the workload identity, permitted destination, policy rule, and decision, while avoiding sensitive request bodies. Count denied and allowed connections by service and owner. A sudden allowed connection to a permitted wildcard can be more useful evidence than a blocked request to an unknown address.
Try a direct IP connection, a mismatched TLS server name, an alternate port, and a destination reached through a redirect. Confirm that the policy follows the same trust path the application would use. Test from a pod, a node, and a serverless function if they share the same account. A control that works in one runtime may not exist in another.
Run a canary that attempts to reach an unapproved test domain and verify the denial is recorded. Then exercise each approved integration after a certificate rotation, DNS change, and provider outage. An allowlist that breaks recovery tools or blocks a trusted patching service may be removed under operational pressure unless the exception process is clear.
The final control is a small, reviewable set of destinations with an owner and a reason. Egress restriction is not a promise that a compromised service cannot communicate. It is a way to make that communication require an approved route and leave a record of which workload used it.
Istio: Accessing external services and egress control
Istio: Egress gateways
Gateway API backend security guidance

articles.title: How an Instagram Engagement Rate Calculator Works (Formulas + JS)
articles.description:
How an Instagram Engagement Rate Calculator Works (Formulas + JS)


Follower count is the number people see first. Engagement rate is the number that tells you whether content is doing its job. Two accounts with the same follower total can sit miles apart on engagement: one gets a few likes per post, the other pulls comments, saves and shares on almost every upload.
This post walks through the three formulas most Instagram calculators use, the edge cases that break naive math, and a small JavaScript snippet you can drop into a page or notebook. No API keys required. Everything here uses numbers you can pull from a public profile or from Instagram Insights on a professional account.
For a feed post, most calculators count some mix of:
likes
comments
saves
shares
Stories add replies and sticker taps. Reels often lean hard on plays, likes, comments and shares. Profile visits and link taps are useful too, but they are harder to get from outside Insights, so public calculators usually stick to the four post actions above.
The important idea is ratio, not raw volume. Five hundred likes on a 200,000-follower account is weak. One hundred twenty likes on a 1,500-follower account is strong.
This is the public default. Anyone can compute it from a profile without Insights access.
ER_followers = (likes + comments + saves + shares) / followers * 100

Example: a post gets 300 likes, 25 comments, 40 saves and 15 shares → 380 interactions. The account has 8,000 followers.
380 / 8000 * 100 = 4.75%

Strength: easy to compare accounts from the outside.
Weakness: many followers never see a given post. If Instagram only showed the post to 1,200 of those 8,000 people, the follower-based rate understates how well the content worked for the people who actually saw it.
Reach is the number of unique accounts that saw the post. You get it from Insights.
ER_reach = total_interactions / reach * 100

Same post, 380 interactions, reach of 1,200:
380 / 1200 * 100 ≈ 31.7%

That looks huge next to 4.75%, and that is the point. Reach-based rate answers a different question: of the people who saw this, how many acted?
Use this when you are tuning content. Use the follower version when you are comparing public profiles.
Impressions count every view, including repeats from the same account.
ER_impressions = total_interactions / impressions * 100

If the same post had 1,800 impressions (some people saw it twice), then:
380 / 1800 * 100 ≈ 21.1%

Impressions-based rate sits between the other two when reach is lower than impressions, which is the usual case. It is useful for Reels and ads, where repeat views are common. For organic feed posts, reach is usually the cleaner denominator.



Goal
Prefer




Compare public accounts
by followers


Improve your own content
by reach


Ads / Reels with heavy repeats
by impressions



A calculator that offers all three, and labels them clearly, beats one that hides the formula. Pick one method for your dashboard and stick to it week to week so the trend line means something.
Division by zero. Guard it. Return null, 0, or a clear "not enough data" message. Never show Infinity or NaN in a UI.
Saves and shares are not visible on someone else's public profile. Outside calculators often fall back to likes + comments only. Say so in the UI, or the number will look lower than an Insights-backed calculator for the same post.
A carousel can rack up high saves. A Reel can rack up high shares and plays. If you mix formats in one average without labeling them, a "bad" week of carousels can look like a "good" week of Reels, or the reverse. Average by format when you can.
One post with 40% reach-based engagement will drag a 12-post average into fantasy land. Median across recent posts is often more honest than mean. At minimum, show both the average and the latest-post value.
Instagram periodically removes inactive accounts. A sudden follower drop with flat engagement is often cleanup, not a content failure. Conversely, a bought or contest-driven follower spike tanks follower-based ER overnight even when the content did not change. Reach-based ER usually stays steadier through those swings.
Engagement keeps trickling in for days. Calculating ER one hour after posting understates the final number. For fair comparisons, use a fixed window (for example, 48 hours after publish) or wait until Insights marks the post as settled.
Here is a minimal function that covers the three formulas and the zero-denominator case. No dependencies.
/**
 * @param {object} input
 * @param {number} input.likes
 * @param {number} input.comments
 * @param {number} [input.saves=0]
 * @param {number} [input.shares=0]
 * @param {number} [input.followers]
 * @param {number} [input.reach]
 * @param {number} [input.impressions]
 * @returns {{ byFollowers: number|null, byReach: number|null, byImpressions: number|null, interactions: number }}
 */
function engagementRates({
  likes = 0,
  comments = 0,
  saves = 0,
  shares = 0,
  followers,
  reach,
  impressions,
} = {}) {
  const interactions = likes + comments + saves + shares;

  const pct = (num, den) =>
    typeof den === "number" && den > 0
      ? Math.round((num / den) * 10000) / 100 // two decimals
      : null;

  return {
    interactions,
    byFollowers: pct(interactions, followers),
    byReach: pct(interactions, reach),
    byImpressions: pct(interactions, impressions),
  };
}

// example
console.log(
  engagementRates({
    likes: 300,
    comments: 25,
    saves: 40,
    shares: 15,
    followers: 8000,
    reach: 1200,
    impressions: 1800,
  })
);
// → { interactions: 380, byFollowers: 4.75, byReach: 31.67, byImpressions: 21.11 }

Round to two decimals for display. Keep full precision internally if you are charting trends.
function averageByFollowers(posts) {
  const rates = posts
    .map((p) => engagementRates(p).byFollowers)
    .filter((r) => r !== null);

  if (!rates.length) return null;
  const sum = rates.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  return Math.round((sum / rates.length) * 100) / 100;
}

Same pattern works for reach and impressions. For a sturdier number, sort rates and take the middle value (median) instead of the mean.
These are ballpark ranges people use when reading follower-based ER. They shift by niche, format and account size, so use them as context, not a grade:
under ~1%: quiet for most small accounts
~1–3%: common for mid-size accounts
~3–6%: solid for many creator niches
above ~6%: strong, especially past 10k followers
Reach-based numbers run much higher. Do not mix the two scales in one sentence.
If you wire this into a form:
Require likes, comments and at least one denominator.
Label which formula you used next to the result.
Note when saves/shares were omitted.
Offer a "last 12 posts average" mode so one viral post cannot dominate.
That is the whole engine behind most Instagram engagement rate calculators: three ratios, a few guards, and clear labels. Once you can compute it yourself, you can trust (or challenge) any number a tool shows you.
For a free browser version of the same math, try the Muddlefox engagement rate calculator. More Instagram and TikTok guides live at https://muddlefox.com/.

articles.title: MySQL or PostgreSQL, Does It Matter to Choose Which?
articles.description:
When we develop a program, or an app, it is important to keep our data on some place. If you learn basic web app programming from Youtube or from other learning platform, you will be guided to choose MySQL as a starter database. MySQL is beginner friendly, easy to use, and versatile when it comes to intermediate level query. But there is other SQL version, which is PostgreSQL. So what is the difference between those two?
SQL is Structured Query Language. It is a programming language of which we can use to manage MySQL and PostgreSQL. MySQL and PostgreSQL is a database management system. Those two are the places we can store the database, and SQL is the language we can use to access them.
The learning curve of SQL is quite lean. The core concept of the query is simple. But when it comes to complexes database which have tons of tables, it is quite challenging to optimize the syntax of the query. SQL language is quite a lot to explore, but we can grasp the core of SQL quite easy.
For example, the JOIN syntax. There are many kind of JOIN syntax like INNER JOIN or OUTER JOIN which have different purposes, but the concept is the same, to join the columns of the tables. Same as INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE, quite explanatory each of those syntax for the SQL.
MySQL is commonly used with web application, mostly with PHP and Javascript. Web applications store their user data, config data, and application data within MySQL. In PHP, they have mysqli extension which for some PHP installation is enabled by default. It is the interface for the web application to execute SQL Query to MySQL databases. The query which executed then returns output to the web application or changes data in the database.
But when you familiar with enterprise application like ERP or HRIS, you will heard PostgreSQL much more often. PostgreSQL is a database, just like MySQL. They have quite similar query syntax on INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, but on some cases like incremental key, upsert, or concatenate, they have different syntax. PostgreSQL much optimized for bigger application for which they have optimized for larger databases and more complex queries.
Well, yes basically. PostgreSQL is more optimized to larger and complex databases.
The truth of deciding of which database to choose is based on what exactly the specifications do you need?
If you only need database for simple web application for about 100 users which not concurrently using, it is better to use MySQL. The installation is simple and will fulfill your app's need. MySQL interface on some programming language mostly pre-installed so it won't be too much of a hassle to install your database.
But if you need a more heavy load transaction and computation, most likely because your app used by a lot of concurrent users and maybe you will be using pgvector to use LLMs, you will need PostgreSQL. It is more optimized for larger JOINs for much more relational tables and even can be setup as Vector Database for your LLMs.
The more we know the capacity of those two database system, the better our app will perform.

articles.title: What the Zeabur Breach Actually Broke (and What Isolation Architecture Could Have Stopped)
articles.description:
What the Zeabur Breach Actually Broke (and What Isolation Architecture Could Have Stopped)


The Zeabur breach ended the company. Taiwan-based hosting platform Zeabur disclosed a second major security incident on October 14-15, 2026, seven weeks after its first, and founder Yuanlin Lin announced on October 17 that Zeabur would shut down entirely by December 31. The root cause wasn't a zero-day. It was a publicly reachable admin interface and credentials that were never rotated.
Jump to the specific architecture choices that turned one compromise into every customer's problem if you're evaluating a hosting platform right now.
The August 27, 2026 incident started small. According to Zeabur's own incident report, an attacker exploited an authorization flaw in NextChat, an AI chat application one customer had deployed on Zeabur's shared cluster. BleepingComputer's reporting describes what happened next: the attacker moved from that single compromised application through poorly isolated internal systems, obtained a root AWS key, and read part of Zeabur's production database, including account information and environment variables holding other customers' third-party API keys and database passwords.
That sentence, "moved through poorly isolated internal systems," is the entire story in miniature. One customer's vulnerable application became a pivot point into the hosting provider's own management plane. In a correctly isolated multi-tenant system, a bug in any single tenant's workload should never grant a path into the infrastructure that runs every other tenant's workload, regardless of how badly that one tenant's code is written.
Zeabur's own preliminary report lays out the October 14-15 chain in granular detail, and it's worth reading because the specifics matter more than the summary. The company confirms the admin tokens for its shared cluster "had no expiry" and had not been rotated since January 2024, stored in plaintext in a private configuration repository, with the admin interface itself reachable from the public internet.
An attacker used those credentials to access the shared cluster across nine regions, then ran read commands inside 865 customer database containers, mostly n8n and PostgreSQL instances, between October 14, 13:40 UTC and 17:04 UTC. A second, separate path targeted GCP servers Zeabur manages on customers' behalf as "dedicated" infrastructure: the attacker signed in as root to 101 of them, using root passwords that were, again, stored in plaintext in the servers' initialization settings. Zeabur confirms the attacker added SSH keys to 50 of those servers for persistence and attached copies of customer disks to attacker-controlled virtual machines.
The two paths converged when the attacker used stolen internal-network admin credentials, obtained from the shared-cluster path, to add a node to Zeabur's private network from a compromised GCP server. From there, a flat internal network let that single node reach the platform database directly. Zeabur confirmed 29 database connections and 8,903 traceable operations in the roughly 37 minutes before the node was removed, exposing 321,810 accounts and about 3.2 million environment variable records.
Here's the detail that should worry anyone who thinks a post-incident credential rotation is sufficient on its own: Zeabur's own report states plainly that the cluster admin tokens and GCP keys used in the October breach "were not included in the post-August rotation." The company rotated what it believed the first attacker had touched. It didn't rotate every credential that could reach the same blast radius, because the blast radius itself, a flat internal network where one admin credential unlocks nine regions and 101 servers, was never redrawn between the two incidents.
Bank Info Security's reporting adds that Zeabur's working theory is that the October credentials trace back to a GitHub App private key stolen in the August breach, left unchanged in a repository even after other keys were rotated. If that theory holds, both breaches share a single root: one secret, once exposed, kept paying out for seven more weeks because nobody could be certain everything downstream of it had actually been replaced.
None of this required a novel exploit. Every step is a known category of mistake, stacked:
A tenant's workload could reach the provider's internal network at all. The August NextChat compromise should have ended at the boundary of that one customer's container. It didn't, because the internal systems behind it were, in Zeabur's own words, poorly isolated.
Admin credentials for multi-tenant infrastructure had no expiry. Tokens unused for over two years, since January 2024, remained valid for an admin interface controlling nine regions.
That admin interface was reachable from the public internet. Not VPN-gated, not IP-allowlisted: reachable by anyone who had the token, from anywhere.
Credentials were stored in plaintext rather than a secrets manager. A compromised repository was enough; no additional decryption step stood in the way.
The internal network was flat. One node, added from one compromised server, could reach the platform database holding every customer's data.
"Dedicated" servers still depended on a shared, plaintext root password the provider controlled. Customers paying for isolated infrastructure were still exposed to a single leaked key held by the platform operator.
Our verdict: none of these six gaps are exotic. They're the same checklist every infrastructure security review already asks about. The lesson isn't that Zeabur was uniquely careless; it's that a platform can look secure in its marketing and still fail every one of these checks simultaneously, and the only way a customer finds out is after the breach, not before.
Can a compromised customer workload reach the provider's own management plane? If the answer involves "poorly isolated internal systems," that's the single biggest predictor of blast radius in this incident and in most multi-tenant breaches.
Are admin and infrastructure credentials short-lived, or do they have no expiry? A credential with no expiry is a liability that compounds for as long as it exists, used or not.
Is the admin interface reachable from the public internet, or gated behind a private network? Zeabur's was public. A provider that can't answer this clearly hasn't thought about it.
Does your "dedicated" server actually eliminate the provider's standing access, or just the other customers' access? If the provider holds a master root credential for infrastructure you're paying to have isolated, you've reduced one risk and kept another.
Is the internal network segmented, or flat? A flat network turns any single compromised credential into access to everything behind it, which is exactly how 865 database containers and 101 servers both ended up exposed from what started as one customer's chat app.
What caused the Zeabur breach?
Two separate incidents, seven weeks apart, and neither one was a single bug. The first, in August 2026, started when an attacker exploited a flaw in a customer's NextChat application and moved through poorly isolated internal systems into Zeabur's infrastructure. The second, in October, used plaintext admin credentials with no expiry, never rotated since January 2024, to access a publicly reachable admin interface and reach the platform database.
Why is Zeabur shutting down after the breach?
Founder Yuanlin Lin announced on October 17, 2026 that Zeabur would wind down entirely by December 31, citing both security incidents alongside unsustainable growth and architectural complexity that the company's small team could not keep pace with, however much it tried to patch around the gaps after each incident.
Did rotating credentials after the first Zeabur breach prevent the second one?
No, and that's the uncomfortable part. Zeabur's own report states the admin tokens and cloud keys used in the October breach were not included in the rotation performed after the August incident, meaning the same underlying exposure window remained open for seven more weeks.
We pulled Zeabur's own official incident report in full, cross-referenced the technical chain against BleepingComputer's and Bank Info Security's independent reporting, and confirmed the timeline (August 27 first incident, October 14-15 second incident, October 17 shutdown announcement) matches across all three sources. The theory linking the two breaches to a single leaked GitHub App key is explicitly labeled a working hypothesis by Zeabur itself, not a confirmed fact, and we've kept that qualification rather than stating it as settled.
I'm Rohit, founder of Krova Cloud: every Cube boots with no public IP until you open a port yourself, and our own infrastructure has no standing path from a customer's workload back into our management plane, because that path is exactly what turned one vulnerable chat app into a seven-week, 321,810-account cascade for someone else. More debugging stories at debugly.dev.

articles.title: 作図ツールで作るマトリクス図のメンテがつらいのでYAMLから自動生成するCLIツールを作りました
articles.description:
はじめに
#
開発計画などの全体像を表現する際に用いられることが多い2次元マトリクス図。多くの場合、オフィスソフトや作図ツールで作成されます。
そこでYAMLで定義したマトリクスデータをもとにイメージファイルを生成するNode.jsのCLIツール（matrix-renderer）を公開しました。
本記事では、このツールを作った背景や具体的な使い方について紹介します。
出力例

GitHubリポジトリ
npmパッケージ
作成のきっかけ
#
あるタスクでガイドやツールの提供状況を明示するため、X軸にフェーズ、Y軸に技術的な関心領域（アプリ、インフラ、プロセスetc）をとるマトリクスが作成されていました。
プロジェクトへの展開も考えていましたが、残念ながらSVGが使えずリンク要件を満たせなかったため、展開は断念。
類似するツールとの違い
#
オフィスソフトや作図ツールと比べて得意なことと苦手なこと。
得意なこと
#
継続的な更新がしやすい

更新対象がYAMLなので変更しやすく、差分管理もしやすい
更新と連動した公開が可能

CLIツールなので、ビルドスクリプトやCI/CDパイプラインに組み込むことでYAMLファイルの更新をトリガーにしてイメージ生成できます。
デプロイもCI/CDパイプラインに組み込めば、YAMLファイルの更新からイメージ公開までを自動化できます。
レイアウトは自動配置が基本

X軸、Y軸は等間隔で自動設定します。
指定されたX軸の開始列/終了列およびY軸の行にアイテムを配置します。
同一Y軸内で空いている領域があった場合は、アイテムを自動配置します。
同じ行のアイテム同士で期間が重なる場合は、表示が重ならないよう縦方向に配置します。
アイテムからのリンク

SVGのみですが、アイテムへのURL埋め込みに対応しています。
苦手なこと
#
レイアウトの自由度が低い

特定のX軸、Y軸の幅は等間隔でカスタマイズできない
同一Y軸内は自動配置するため、アイテム前後関係を付けるようなことはできない。
多様な図形を用いた作図などは対応してない
利用シーン
#
以下のような「2軸で物事を分類・マッピングし、継続的にドキュメントとして公開したい」ケースに最適です。
フェーズ × 技術分類でツールやガイド管理
組織の技術領域 × 習熟度/採用フェーズ（Adopt, Trial, Assess, Holdなど）で技術スタックの習熟度管理
対応段階（平常時、検知、初動、原因調査、復旧、振り返り）× 担当領域で障害対応の手順やツールをマッピング
部門 × 分類でシステム、機能の一覧
使い方
#
実行環境
#
Node.js 24+
YAMLを用意する
#
以下は、開発フェーズごとにガイドやツールを配置する入力ファイル例です。
こちらを参照してください。
title: 社内標準DevOpsツールチェーン & 開発ガイドマップ

  label: 開発フェーズ
  values:
    - label: 要件定義・計画
      color: "#e8f8f5"

      color: "#eaf2f8"
    - label: テスト・検証
      color: "#ebf5fb"

      color: "#fdfefe"

  - id: git-guide
    label: GitHub・Git利用規約ガイド

    label: Datadog監視ダッシュボード
    lane: インフラ・CI/CD
    from: 運用・監視
    to: 運用・監視

アイテム
ID、表示名、配置する行、開始列、終了列、色、URL




アイテムはlaneで配置する行を、fromとtoで開始列および終了列を指定します。
同じ行のアイテム同士で期間が重なる場合は、表示が重ならないよう縦方向に配置します。
xAxis.valuesとyAxis.valuesに書いた順番が、イメージ上の表示順になります。
イメージ幅（width）、色（color）、URL（url）は省略可としています。
イメージファイルを生成する
#
YAMLファイルからイメージファイルを生成するコマンド例は下記の通りです。
こちらを参照してください。
# 1. 入力ファイルのみ指定
npx matrix-renderer render -- docs/matrices/matrix.yaml

# 2. 出力ファイル名を指定
npx matrix-renderer render -- docs/matrices/matrix.yaml --out public/images/development-guide

# 3. 出力ファイル種類を指定
npx matrix-renderer render -- docs/matrices/matrix.yaml --out public/images/development-guide --out-type svg


  


1: 入力ファイルと同じフォルダーにイメージを生成します。

docs/matrices/matrix.png
docs/matrices/matrix.svg
2: 指定されたディレクトリ/ファイル名でイメージを生成します。

public/images/development-guide.png
public/images/development-guide.svg
3: 指定されたファイル種類のみ生成します。

public/images/development-guide.svg
CI/CDに組み込む
#
GitHub ActionsなどのCI/CDワークフローに生成コマンドを追加すれば、YAMLの変更に合わせてイメージを再生成できます。
name: Build documentation

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - "docs/matrices/**"
      - ".github/workflows/docs.yml"

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Render matrix images
        run: npx --yes matrix-renderer@0.1.2 render -- docs/matrices/development-guide.yaml --out public/images/development-guide
      # このあとデプロイを実施


  


まとめ
#
matrix-rendererを使うと、YAMLで定義したマトリクスデータからPNGおよびSVGを生成できます。
ツール自体が公開サイトへのデプロイを行うわけではありませんが、CI/CDに組み込むことでYAML更新からデプロイまで自動化できます。
自由なレイアウトよりも、マトリクスを継続的に更新したい場合にDoc as Codeの選択肢として活用できます。

articles.title: 素のClaude CodeとTDDで初見のお題に挑む ― TDDBC仙台11thのセッションログを公開します
articles.description:
このブログエントリは、初見のコーディング課題に対して私が素の Claude Code（Skill やプラグインは不使用）とテスト駆動開発で取り組んだ約4時間20分のセッションログを、ほぼ編集せずに整形して記事化したものです。実際に入力したプロンプトだけでなく、AIとの協業において人間がいつ何をどう判断したかが残っています。長い記事なので、拾い読みのためのリンク集（目次、私が判断を下した場面、プロンプト一覧）を冒頭と末尾に用意しました。コーディング課題の内容と、私が書いたコードは下記のリンクで公開されています。
TDDBC Sendai 11th モルックの得点記録（最初からSTEP 03まで）
twada/tddbc-sendai-11th: TDDBC Sendai 11th のお題に Claude Code でチャレンジした記録
なお、セッションログ以外の地の文は私が手で書いています。リンク集の作成は Claude に手伝ってもらっています。もちろん、このブログエントリの大部分はセッションログで、その大部分は Claude が生成したものです。
背景
テスト駆動開発の体験型ワークショップ TDD Boot Camp（TDDBC） を久しぶりに仙台で開催しました。TDDBC では、午後のワークショップパートで参加者がペアになりペアプログラミングを行います。今年はコーディングエージェントを使っても使わなくてもよしとしました。利用割合としては半々だったように思います。
普段の TDDBC では私はコーディング課題の出題者の立場なのですが、TDDBC 仙台では主催チームの井上さんがコーディング課題を考案するので、私も参加者として初見のお題にチャレンジする密かな楽しみがあります。ただ、例年は各ペアのレビューに歩き回るので、出題されたばかりのお題に開催中の会場でチャレンジする余力はありませんでした。しかし、今年は Claude Code があります。各ペアの机を回る合間に Claude Code に指示を出せば、片手間（おそらくスピードは 1/3 くらい）ではありますが、私も当日にお題にチャレンジ可能になると考え、実際にやってみました。
その後 TDDBC の懇親会 LT でコミット履歴の公開や書いたコードの説明をしましたが、実は参加者の皆様からの要望が一番多かったのがプロンプトの公開でした。プロンプトは GitHub 上の履歴に残りません。書いたコードよりも、そのコードが出てくるきっかけのプロンプトが知りたいのはよくわかります。
ということで、このブログエントリでは、私が各ペアのレビューの合間に Claude Code と開発を行った際のセッションログを整形し、実際に私が出した指示や Claude Code の返答を読めるような形式にしてみました。なお、セッションログの変換プログラムも Claude Code で開発しました。
繰り返しになりますが、当日出題分のお題や、私が実際に書いた（書かせた）コードは GitHub で公開されています。また、当日は到達できませんでしたが、お題の全体（最後のSTEPまで）も公開されています。
ブログエントリの編集方針について
このセッションログは、当日 13:12 から 17:34 までの約4時間20分の開発（各ペアの机をレビューで回りながらなので片手間ですが）をほぼそのまま収録しています。
TDDBC の懇親会で要望をいただいたのはプロンプトの公開でしたが、プロンプトだけを抜き出しても、その意味はおそらく伝わりません。 Claude が何を提案し、それを見て私が何をしたかという文脈が無いからです。
編集して要所だけを残すと、上手くいった場面を切り出したハイライト集になってしまいます。実際の開発には、混ざってしまったコミットを後から PR に分け直したり、コミットの順番を入れ替えたりといった地味な作業も含まれます。そうした進め方も含めて、生に近い形で残しました。
AI でのコーディングについての記事は増えていますが、そのほとんどは結果の紹介か、「こう書くと良い」というノウハウの要約であり、実際のセッションを編集せずに数時間分丸ごと見せた記録は、まだ少ないのではないかと思います。このエントリは「いつ、何を見て、どう判断したか」を記しています。これは要約すると消えてしまう類いの情報です。
読み方
長いブログエントリなので、全部を読む必要はありません。目的に合わせて次のような読み方ができるのではないかと思います。
流れだけ知りたい場合は、下記の目次と「私が判断を下した場面」を読み、気になるところに飛んでみてください
プロンプトを知りたい場合は、「User」のセクションだけを読んでみてください。記事の末尾には、各プロンプトへのリンク付きの一覧を付けています
AIとの協業の実際を知りたい場合は、 Claude の返答や思考プロセスも含めて、頭から読んでみてください
それでも長いと感じた場合には、このブログエントリを AI に読ませてみてください。単に要約させるよりも、「人間が判断を下した場面を、直前の Claude の提案と並べて抜き出してください」のように、知りたいことを指定して頼むのがおすすめです。AI との開発記録を AI に読み解かせるのも、いまどきの読み方なのだと思います。
目次
開発の段階ごとの目次です。時刻は当日の開始時刻です。
 時刻 
 段階 
 内容 




 13:12 
 環境準備 
 技術スタックを指定してプロジェクトを準備。コミット規約と「Red/Green TDD で進める」を CLAUDE.md に書き、お題を保存 


 13:32 
 STEP 01-1：1本倒した場合 
 スキットルの表現や範囲外の入力の扱いを議論し、古典的 TDD で実装。型レベルテストも追加 


 13:56 
 PR の分割 
 混ざってしまった環境準備と STEP 01-1 を、2つの Stacked PR に分ける 


 14:07 
 STEP 01-2：2本以上倒した場合、1本も倒さなかった場合 
 「2本倒した」のモデリングと、同じスキットルの重複を議論。検証方針の ADR を改定 


 14:50 
 STEP 02：現在の得点を求める 
 得点を「毎回、投てきの履歴全体から合計する」方針を議論で決めて実装 


 16:01 
 品質保証（その1） 
 コードカバレッジの取得、Mutation Testing の追加、GitHub Actions による CI を導入 


 16:24 
 STEP 03：得点の推移を確認する 
 結果配列の中身を議論し、scoreHistoryOf を実装 


 17:03 
 品質保証（その2） 
 node:assert による表明プログラミングと、Property-based Testing を導入 





私が判断を下した場面
私が判断を下した場面をいくつか挙げます。
13:32 コードを書く前に設計を議論する: 「まだコードは書かないでください」と指示し、設計に合意してから計画、そして TDD に進む流れを作る。スキットルの番号と点数が同じ number 型なのは嫌だという違和感も最初に伝える。


結果: スキットルを番号を持つオブジェクトで包み、点数は pointsOf 関数で求め、範囲外の番号は実行時に検証せず型だけで防ぐ設計に合意する。
13:56 混ざった作業を PR に分け直す: 環境準備と STEP 01-1 を同じブランチで進めてしまったことに後から気づき、2つの PR に分割させる。STEP 01-1 の PR は、環境準備の PR の上に積む形（Stacked PR）にする。
14:13 重複したスキットルをどう扱うか: Claude が挙げた論点を基に「各番号のスキットルは1本ずつ」を型で表現できないかをまず調査させる。型で重複を検出すると、誤検出したり引数の順序で結果が変わったりすることが分かる。


結果: Claude は「集合として扱う（重複は1本と数える）」案を推奨するが、私は不正な状態ならば速やかに失敗させる fail fast の原則に従い、実行時エラーにする案を採用する。あわせて ADR の方針を「可能な限り静的に検証し、ダメであれば実行時に検証する」に改定する。
15:07 お題に書かれていないことを決める: Claude が整理した論点に一つずつ答えたうえで、「テストリストは若干足りない」と押し返す。


結果: 「投てき 0 回」と「1回投てきして 0 本」の区別、得点に上限がないことのテスト、エラーのときに途中までの得点を返さないことなどが加わり、テストリストは10項目になる。
16:35 2つの案を賛否両論で比較させる: 戻り値のモデリングについて、得点の推移を表す配列として [5, 16, 16, 19] と [5, 11, 0, 3] の2案を挙げ、それぞれ賛成と反対の両方の立場から論じさせ、証拠の強さで比較させる。


結果: Claude は、お題の文面・例・用語という強い証拠に支えられているのは前者の [5, 16, 16, 19] だと結論づけ、私もその案を採用する。
17:03 型で守っていても実行時の表明を足す: 型レベルで担保済みのスキットル番号について、実行時にノーガードなのは避けたいので node:assert による表明を加える。


結果: mutation score 100% の基準とぶつかる点は、表明を変異の対象から外すことで解消し、「検証」と「表明」を区別する ADR を新しく起草する。
開発環境
Claude
開発は Claude Desktop の Code タブ（Claude Desktop に組み込まれた Claude Code）で行いました。セッションログに記録されていた設定は以下の通りです（Claude Desktop のバージョンはログに残っていないため、アプリの表示から転記しています）。
 項目 
 値

 3.6556.2 (20c019) 


 Claude Code 
 2.1.308 


 モデル 
 Claude Opus 5.5（claude-opus-5-5） 


 Effort 
 high 


 Thinking 
 adaptive（要約表示） 


 権限モード

 応答言語

Fast mode は使っていません。セッションログ中の「思考プロセス」は、Thinking の表示設定が要約表示（summarized）だったため、思考そのものではなく要約されたものです。
ハーネスと使用ツール
今回の開発では、Skill、プラグイン、フック等は使っていません。CLAUDE.md も無い状態から始め、素のモデルの賢さと、あとは私の指示だけで TDD を回しています。
エージェント制御のためのハーネスは決定的なツールだけで構成されています。プログラミング言語は TypeScript（型チェッカーは tsc）、テストは Node 組み込みの node:test と power-assert、コードカバレッジ測定も Node 組み込みの node:test、 linter/formatter は oxlint/oxfmt、 Mutation Testing は Stryker、 Property-based Testing は fast-check、表明プログラミングには Node 組み込みの node:assert を使っています。バージョンはそれぞれ下記のものです。

# 0002. TypeScript をコンパイルせず Node の type stripping で直接実行する

- ステータス: 承認済み
- 日付: 2026-10-24

## コンテキスト

TDD のサイクル(Red → Green → Refactor)は短く回せるほど良い。テスト実行の前にトランスパイルやバンドルの工程があると、待ち時間と設定の複雑さが増える。

Node 26 では type stripping(型注釈を取り除いて実行する機能)がフラグなしで使える。ただし対象は「消去可能な構文(erasable syntax)」のみで、Node は `tsconfig.json` を読まない。

代替案:

- `tsc` でビルドしてから `dist/` を実行する — 工程が増え、ソースマップの扱いも必要になる。
- tsx / tsimp などのローダーを使う — 依存が増える。Node 標準機能で足りるなら不要。

## 決定

- `.ts` ファイルを Node でそのまま実行する。ビルド成果物は作らない。
- type stripping と矛盾しないよう、`tsconfig.json` で以下を有効にする。
  - `erasableSyntaxOnly`: `enum`、`namespace`、コンストラクタの parameter properties など、実行時コードを生む TS 固有構文を禁止する。
  - `verbatimModuleSyntax`: 型だけの import は `import type` と書くことを強制する。
  - `allowImportingTsExtensions` + `noEmit`: import パスに `.ts` 拡張子を書く(例: `import { hello } from "../hello.ts"`)。
  - `module: "nodenext"`: Node の ESM 解決規則に合わせる。

## 結果

- テストは `node --test` だけで実行でき、ビルド待ちがない。
- `enum` などの構文は使えない。列挙はユニオン型や `as const` オブジェクトで表現する。
- 型エラーがあってもテストは実行できてしまうため、型検査は別工程で行う(ADR 0006)。
EOF

# 0004. アサーションに @power-assert/node を使う

- ステータス: 承認済み
- 日付: 2026-10-24

## コンテキスト

TDD では「テストが失敗したときに、なぜ失敗したかがすぐ分かる」ことが重要。一方で、学習の焦点を API の暗記ではなく振る舞いの記述に置くため、覚えるアサーション API は少ないほうが良い。

`@power-assert/node` は Node のモジュールフックとして動作し、`node:assert` の `assert(式)` が失敗したとき、式の各部分の値を図示する。

## 決定

- アサーションは `node:assert/strict` を使い、`@power-assert/node` を `node --import @power-assert/node` で読み込む。
- テストの基本形は `assert(actual === expected)` とする。オブジェクトや配列の比較など、必要に応じて `assert.deepEqual` なども使ってよい。
- `@power-assert/node` は内部で Node の実験的 API を使うため、実行のたびに `ExperimentalWarning` が出る。テスト出力を読みやすく保つため、テスト実行時に `--disable-warning=ExperimentalWarning` を付ける。
- 失敗時のスタックトレースを `.ts` の行番号で表示するため `--enable-source-maps` を付ける。

## 結果

- `assert(式)` だけで、失敗時に分かりやすいメッセージが得られる。
- `--disable-warning=ExperimentalWarning` は他の実験的機能の警告もまとめて隠す。警告を確認したいときはフラグなしで `node --test` を直接実行する。
EOF

- ステータス: 承認済み

## コンテキスト

TDD のリファクタリング段階では、静的解析と自動整形を頻繁に回す。ESLint + Prettier は実績があるが、設定と依存が多い。oxlint / oxfmt は Rust 製で高速、かつ設定が少なくて済む。

- コマンド: `npm run lint`、`npm run fmt`(整形)、`npm run fmt:check`(差分検出のみ)。

## 結果

- lint / format が一瞬で終わり、サイクルを妨げない。
- ESLint / Prettier のエコシステム(独自ルールやプラグイン)は直接は使えない。ルールが不足したら ADR を追加して見直す。

- ステータス: 承認済み

- `npm run check` で typecheck → lint → fmt:check → test をまとめて実行できるようにする。

## 結果

- 実行(type stripping)と型検査(tsc)の役割がはっきり分かれる。
- `npm test` が通っても型エラーが残っている場合があるため、コミット前には `npm run check` を実行する。

# モルックの得点記録

小さなテストから始めて、モルックの得点計算を段階的に育てていきましょう。

このお題は、[TDDBC Sendai 11th](https://tddbc.connpass.com/event/407078/)（2026-10-24）のために作成しました。

## モルック（Mölkky）とは

モルックは、複数のチームが得点を競い合うゲームです。各チームが順番に投てきを行い、得点を積み重ねていきます。

モルックでは、1〜12の番号（スキットル番号、skittle number）が付いた木製のピン「スキットル（skittle）」を使用します。各番号のスキットルは1本ずつあり、全部で12本です。

木製の棒「モルック（mölkky）」を投げてスキットルを倒すことを「投てき（throw）」と呼びます。

## 進め方

各STEPで公開された仕様だけを対象に、テスト駆動開発（Red → Green → Refactor）で実装してください。

- ペアで相談しながら進めてください。
- AIを使うかどうかは、ペアで決めてください。
- お題に書かれていないモルックのルールは、存在しないものとして扱ってください。実際のモルックのルールを知っていても適用しません。先のSTEPを想定して機能を作り込む必要もありません。
- コード例はSTEP 01-1・01-2のみに掲載しています。呼び出し例であり、クラス名・メソッド名や内部設計を指定するものではありません。
- 書かれているルールの範囲で決まっていないこと（入力の扱い、エラーの表現方法など）は、ペアで相談して決め、その決定をテストとして残してください。

各STEPの例は、仕様を説明するためのものです。テストリストの手がかりにしてください。

## STEP 01　投てきの点数を計算する

このお題では、まず1チームの投てきを扱います。1回の投てきで得られる点を「点数（points）」と呼びます。点数は、倒れたスキットルによって決まります。

### STEP 01-1：1本倒した場合

1回の投てきでスキットルを1本倒した場合、そのスキットル番号が点数になります。

例えば、5番のスキットルを倒した場合は5点、12番のスキットルを倒した場合は12点です。

```java
new 投てき(5).点数();  // 5
new 投てき(12).点数(); // 12
```

### STEP 01-2：2本以上倒した場合、1本も倒さなかった場合

1回の投てきでスキットルを2本以上倒した場合は、倒したスキットルの本数が点数になります。

1本も倒さなかった場合は0点です。

```java
new 投てき(5, 8).点数(); // 2
new 投てき().点数();     // 0
```

コードはJava風の呼び出し例です。日本語の識別子やクラス構成を指定するものではありません。

# 0007. ドメインモデルは読み取り専用データと純粋関数で表す

- ステータス: 承認済み
- 日付: 2026-10-24

## コンテキスト

お題は STEP ごとに仕様が段階的に公開され、先の仕様は分からない。お題の進め方でも、先の STEP を想定した作り込みはしないことになっている。仕様が変わるたびに設計を素早く直せるよう、ドメインモデルは小さく、変更しやすく保ちたい。

お題のコード例は Java 風(`new 投てき(5).点数()`)だが、クラス構成を指定するものではない。

また、スキットル番号と点数はどちらも数値で表せる。同じ `number` 型にすると、「スキットル番号が点数になる」というルールを経由せずに、番号をそのまま点数として扱えてしまう。

## 決定

- ドメインの値は読み取り専用(`readonly`)のプレーンなオブジェクトや型で表し、振る舞いは純粋関数で書く。クラスは使わない。

- 点数は `type Points = number` の別名とする。足したり比べたりする量なので、ブランド型にはしない。
- 点数の計算は関数 `pointsOf(skittle: Skittle): Points` で行い、「スキットル番号 → 点数」のルールをこの関数に集める。
- 型や関数は、公開済みの仕様を満たすのに必要十分な分だけ作る。新しい仕様が公開されたら、その都度設計を見直す。

- データと計算が分かれているので、テストが書きやすく、仕様変更時に直す範囲を見つけやすい。
- 点数への変換が `pointsOf` を通ることが型で強制され、ルールがコード上で見える。
- `Points` は `number` の別名なので、任意の数値を点数として扱うことは防げない。紛らわしさが問題になったらブランド型への変更を検討する。

# 0009. 入力は可能な限り静的に検証し、できなければ実行時に検証する

- ステータス: 承認済み
- 日付: 2026-10-24
- [ADR 0008](0008-guarantee-skittle-number-range-by-type.md) を置き換える

## コンテキスト

ADR 0008 では、スキットル番号の範囲(1〜12)を型で保証し、実行時には検証しないことにした。

STEP 01-2 で、1 回の投てきで複数のスキットルを倒せるようになった(`pointsOf(...skittles)`)。お題には「各番号のスキットルは1本ずつ」とあるので、`pointsOf(skittle(5), skittle(5))` のように同じ番号が重複した入力は現実には起こりえない。

この重複を型で防げるかを実測した。

- **型レベル計算**(引数のタプル型から重複を検出する): 番号がコンパイル時にリテラルとして分かる場合しか判定できなかった。番号が `SkittleNumber` 全体の値だと誤検出し、引数の順序を入れ替えるだけで結果が変わった。配列を展開した場合は判定できなかった。エラーメッセージも「引数の数が違う」としか表示されなかった。
- **重複を表現できないデータ表現**(番号をキーにしたオブジェクト): 重複は持てなくなるが、呼び出しが `pointsOf({ 5: true, 8: true })` という不自然な形になり、Skittle を中心にした設計(ADR 0007)を作り直す必要がある。

「実行時には検証しない」という方針のままでは、静的に防げない不正な入力に対して、もっともらしい値を返してしまう。

## 決定

- 入力の制約は、可能な限り静的に(型で)検証する。
- 静的に検証できない制約、または信頼できる静的検証が実用的でない制約は、実行時に検証する。
- 各制約の扱いは次のとおり。
  - **スキットル番号の範囲(1〜12)**: 静的に検証できるので、引き続き型(`SkittleNumber`)で保証し、実行時には検証しない。
  - **スキットルの重複**: 型レベル計算は誤検出や順序依存があり信頼できないので、型では検出しない。`pointsOf` が実行時に検証する。
- 実行時の検証に失敗したら、組み込みの `Error` を投げる。メッセージには原因となった値を含める(例: 「スキットル 5 が重複しています」)。重複が複数ある場合は、最初に見つかったものだけを報告する。
- 静的な決定は `@ts-expect-error` を付けた型レベルテストで、実行時の決定は `assert.throws` を使ったテストで残す。

## 結果

- 静的に防げる誤りはコンパイル時に、防げない誤りは実行時に検出され、不正な入力に対してもっともらしい値を返すことがなくなる。
- `pointsOf` は例外を投げうる関数になり、戻り値の型 `Points` だけでは失敗の可能性が表れない。失敗を型で表す必要が出てきたら、Result 型などの導入を新しい ADR で検討する。
- 新しい制約が出てきたら、静的に検証できるか、実用的かをまず検討し、どちらで検証するかを決める。
